RANZCP and eTG recommend combination of a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate) with an atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) for severe acute mania especially with psychotic features; provides faster symptom control than monotherapy (RANZCP CPG 2020; eTG; ASBD).
Lamotrigine has no efficacy in acute mania; for prevention of bipolar depression with slow titration to mitigate SJS risk. Would be correct for bipolar depression prevention (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Pre-lithium baseline includes UEC/eGFR, TFTs, calcium, FBC, pregnancy test, and an ECG (mandatory > 40 years or with cardiac risk factors). Maintenance monitoring includes 12-hour post-dose lithium level at 5-7 days after initiation/dose change, then 3-6 monthly once stable, plus 6-12 monthly renal/thyroid/calcium.
key_points: Therapeutic level: 0.6-0.8 mmol/L maintenance; 0.8-1.0 mmol/L for refractory mania
Toxic > 1.5 mmol/L; severe > 2.0 mmol/L
Standard sample: trough level 12 hours after last dose
Lithium Category D (Ebstein anomaly risk in T1) - fetal cardiac echo at 20 weeks if continued
ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, thiazides, dehydration all raise lithium levels
explanation.pearls: Counsel patients to maintain consistent salt and fluid intake and seek review with any vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, or new medication; subtle tremor, coarse tremor or ataxia signal toxicity.

options.rationale: These are not routine pre-lithium investigations; standard serum creatinine/eGFR adequate for renal screening. (Source: AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines).
Baseline lithium is irrelevant before initiation; renal function plus calcium plus ECG must also be obtained. (Source: AMH).

AMH and eTG Psychotropic require renal function (UEC, eGFR), thyroid function, calcium (lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism), pregnancy test (Category D - Ebstein anomaly risk), and ECG if cardiac risk factors or age > 40; FBC is reasonable baseline (AMH; eTG Psychotropic).
Lithium is renally cleared, not hepatically metabolised; LFTs and ammonia not required. (Source: AMH).
Baseline TFTs and calcium are required at initiation to establish reference; monitored at 6-12 monthly intervals. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity is precipitated by reduced clearance (NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors, dehydration, AKI). Severity is judged by clinical features and level. Haemodialysis indications: level > 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms; > 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features or renal impairment; > 1.5 mmol/L with severe features and inability to excrete.
key_points: Mild toxicity (1.5-2.5 mmol/L): tremor, GI upset, weakness - withhold drug, IV saline, monitor
Severe (> 2.5 mmol/L or symptomatic with renal failure): dialysis
Common precipitants: NSAIDs, thiazides, ACEi/ARB, dehydration, low-salt diet, AKI
Lithium also causes nephrogenic DI, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism with chronic use
Levels rebound post-dialysis: serial levels and often a second session required
explanation.pearls: In a heatwave, counsel lithium patients to maintain hydration and consider holding the dose if vomiting or diarrhoea; brief breaks are safer than waiting until they are ataxic.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium and is not used; lithium must be withheld not dose-reduced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Urinary alkalinisation has minimal effect on lithium elimination; volume replacement is supportive but dialysis is for severe toxicity. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Continuing lithium in severe toxicity is dangerous; priority is removal and renal protection. (Source: AMH).
All three (indapamide, NSAID, dehydration) must be addressed; thiazides increase proximal tubular lithium reabsorption raising levels. Would never be correct as partial (Source: AMH).

Severe lithium toxicity (level > 2.5 mmol/L OR > 2.0 mmol/L with neurological symptoms OR > 1.5 mmol/L with renal impairment) is an indication for haemodialysis per Therapeutic Guidelines; she has neurological compromise, AKI and a 2.4 mmol/L level (Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AMH; Austin Health Poisons).

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1-2 per 1000 births, typically presents in the first 2 weeks postpartum with rapid onset, fluctuating mood, confusion, paranoia and bizarre delusions often involving the baby. It is a psychiatric emergency with significant suicide and infanticide risk. Family history of bipolar disorder is a strong risk factor. Distinguish from baby blues (peaks day 3-5, self-limiting) and PND (gradual onset, mood-predominant).
key_points: Postpartum psychosis: onset typically days 3-14, abrupt, fluctuating, mixed mood/psychotic features
Bipolar family history is the strongest risk factor
Treatment: admit (MBU preferred), antipsychotic +/- mood stabiliser, ECT if severe/refractory
Postnatal depression: gradual onset, mood-predominant, screen with EPDS
Baby blues: peaks day 3-5, self-limiting <2 weeks, no specific treatment
explanation.pearls: Any new-onset psychosis in the first month postpartum is postpartum psychosis until proven otherwise - never discharge home overnight pending review.

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis NOT PND; SSRI monotherapy and outpatient do not address imminent risk to mother/baby. (Source: COPE).
Afebrile, no neuro deficit, normal CRP and strong bipolar family history make PP most likely; LP not first step. Would be correct only with infective features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Discharge of psychotic mother with infant at home is unsafe; benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat psychosis. (Source: COPE).

Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with high suicide and infanticide risk; immediate admission (MBU preferred, general psychiatric ward if MBU unavailable) plus antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone), mood stabiliser if bipolar, and safety planning are standard (COPE; RANZCP; Black Dog Institute).
EPDS screens for depression not psychosis; non-urgent referral is unsafe given imminent risk. (Source: COPE).

explanation.summary: GAD = excessive, hard-to-control worry on most days for at least 6 months PLUS at least 3 of restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance PLUS functional impairment. First-line is CBT; first-line pharmacotherapy when indicated is SSRI or SNRI, started low to mitigate initial anxiogenic effect.
key_points: CBT first-line for mild-moderate GAD
First-line drug: SSRI (escitalopram, sertraline) or SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine)
Start at half the usual depression-starting dose to mitigate initial agitation
Benzodiazepines: <2 weeks only and not first-line
Online CBT (e.g. This Way Up, MindSpot) is PBS-aligned and effective
explanation.pearls: GAD-7 cut-offs: 5 mild, 10 moderate, 15 severe; pair with functional impact when choosing intensity of intervention.

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines not first-line in GAD (dependence risk, chronic course); short courses only for acute crisis. Would be correct only as short-term acute crisis bridge (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Trauma-focused CBT is for PTSD not GAD; she has no trauma. Generic CBT for GAD first-line for mild-moderate but GAD-7 15 with significant impairment warrants combined therapy. Would be correct in PTSD (Source: Phoenix Australia).

GAD-7 15 plus 25 percent loss of work output places her in the moderate-severe band where eTG supports combined first-line therapy; escitalopram is a first-line SSRI for GAD with a favourable side-effect profile (under the 20 mg/day TGA QTc dose-cap), early review captures the 1-2 week activation window during which transient worsening may occur, and CBT remains the durable component.

Mirtazapine not first-line for GAD; SSRI/SNRI are first-line. Mirtazapine reserved for SSRI failure or specific sleep/appetite profile. Would be correct after SSRI failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Lifestyle alone insufficient for GAD-7 15 with functional impairment; mandates structured psychotherapy with/without SSRI. Would be correct only in mild GAD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Panic disorder is diagnosed clinically once medical mimics (arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma, substance intoxication/withdrawal) have been reasonably excluded. Agoraphobia commonly co-exists and shapes treatment (exposure-based CBT critical). First-line treatment is CBT; first-line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI started at low dose.
key_points: Panic attack = abrupt surge of intense fear peaking within minutes, 4+ of 13 symptoms
Panic disorder = recurrent unexpected attacks + 1 month of worry or behaviour change
Agoraphobia: 2+ of public transport, open/enclosed spaces, queues/crowds, alone outside home
First-line: CBT with interoceptive and in vivo exposure; SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram) if drug indicated
Avoid PRN benzodiazepines - they undermine exposure learning
explanation.pearls: Patients with panic disorder frequently present to ED with chest pain; document the screening already done so future ED clinicians can move efficiently to reassurance and follow-up.

options.rationale: GAD has pervasive worry on most days for 6+ months across multiple domains, not discrete episodic surges with phobic avoidance. Would be correct in pervasive worry pattern (Source: DSM-5).
Plasma free metanephrines are screening test of choice and are normal; sustained/paroxysmal HTN, headaches, flushing also absent. Would be correct with elevated metanephrines and HTN (Source: APEG).
Holter and ECGs in symptomatic visits have been normal; in absence of ECG documentation, panic disorder is most likely. Would be correct with ECG-documented paroxysmal AF (Source: Cardiology).

DSM-5 panic disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks (peak within minutes, 4+ symptoms) PLUS at least 1 month of worry about further attacks OR maladaptive behaviour change; agoraphobia is marked fear/avoidance of 2+ of 5 situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues/crowds, alone outside home) (DSM-5; eTG; RANZCP).
TSH is normal (1.8); no tremor, heat intolerance or weight loss to support thyrotoxicosis. Would be correct with suppressed TSH (Source: APEG).

explanation.summary: OCD features ego-dystonic obsessions and time-consuming compulsions with preserved insight, while OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality style of rigidity and perfectionism. PTSD requires an identifiable index trauma plus re-experiencing, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, and hyperarousal for > 1 month. Comorbidity is high in first responders.
key_points: OCD: ego-dystonic, time-consuming (>1 hr/day) compulsions, insight usually preserved
OCPD: ego-syntonic personality style, perfectionism, rigidity, present since young adulthood
PTSD: index trauma + 4 symptom clusters (re-experiencing, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, hyperarousal) > 1 month
Acute stress disorder: same features as PTSD but 3 days - 1 month
Phoenix Australia (formerly ACPMH) is the Australian PTSD authority
explanation.pearls: Always screen first responders, defence and police for both PTSD AND OCD plus AUD - comorbidity is the rule, not the exception.

options.rationale: OCPD is pervasive lifelong pattern of perfectionism/rigidity with limited insight (ego-syntonic); she lacks baseline perfectionism profile. Would be correct in lifelong perfectionism pattern (Source: DSM-5).
GAD has broad worry without ritualised compulsions or trauma re-experiencing; does not fully account. Would be correct in classic GAD (Source: DSM-5).

She meets DSM-5 OCD (intrusive, ego-dystonic obsessions and time-consuming compulsions with insight) AND PTSD (intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, negative cognitions/mood, hyperarousal lasting > 1 month after an index trauma); commonly comorbid in emergency-services workers (Phoenix Australia; RANZCP).
PTSD captures re-experiencing/avoidance/hyperarousal but not ritualised compulsions which independently fit OCD; both present. Would never be correct alone (Source: Phoenix Australia).
Adjustment disorder applies when stressor causes symptoms NOT meeting another disorder; she meets criteria for two specific DSM-5 disorders. (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Phoenix Australia ranks trauma-focused CBT (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR as equally strong first-line treatments for PTSD. Pharmacotherapy (SSRIs sertraline or paroxetine, or SNRI venlafaxine) is second-line or adjunctive. Co-occurring substance use disorder must be managed concurrently, not as a barrier to trauma therapy.
key_points: First-line PTSD: trauma-focused CBT OR EMDR
Second-line pharmacotherapy: sertraline, paroxetine, venlafaxine
Benzodiazepines: avoid (impair extinction learning)
Antipsychotics: not first-line; consider only for refractory psychotic symptoms
Open Arms Veterans and Families Counselling is the major Australian veteran service
explanation.pearls: Prazosin 1-15 mg nocte may help trauma nightmares in selected cases when therapy alone is insufficient (Phoenix Australia).

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines not recommended in PTSD (impair fear extinction critical to trauma-focused therapy, worsen outcomes). (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD).

Phoenix Australia and RANZCP rank trauma-focused CBT (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR as equally strong first-line treatments for PTSD with stronger evidence than pharmacotherapy; co-occurring AUD needs concurrent management (Phoenix Australia PTSD Guidelines 2020).

SSRIs and venlafaxine are second-line behind trauma-focused psychotherapy; reserved for psychotherapy unavailable, ineffective or refused. Would be correct only after psychotherapy unavailable (Source: Phoenix Australia).
Antipsychotics not first-line for core PTSD; low-dose quetiapine for sleep is unsupported with metabolic/movement-disorder risks. (Source: Phoenix Australia).
Single-session debriefing not recommended and may worsen outcomes; structured trauma-focused therapy over multiple sessions required. (Source: Phoenix Australia).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 social anxiety disorder has a performance-only specifier when fear is restricted to public performance. Episodic, situation-specific symptoms with no general social impairment respond well to beta blockade (propranolol) used as required prior to events. Generalised social anxiety is treated with CBT first-line; SSRIs (paroxetine, sertraline, escitalopram) are first-line pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Performance subtype: propranolol 10-40 mg orally 30-60 min pre-event PRN
Generalised social anxiety: CBT first-line; SSRI/SNRI if drug indicated
Avoid beta blockers in asthma, heart block, hypotension, decompensated heart failure
Avoid benzodiazepines for performance (motor/cognitive impairment)
Always pair short-term symptomatic relief with referral for ongoing therapy
explanation.pearls: Trial the propranolol at a similar low-stakes event before the actual audition - some patients get marked bradycardia or fatigue at higher doses.

options.rationale: Performance-only social anxiety responds well to short-term beta blockade (propranolol 10-40 mg about 1 hour pre-event) which blunts peripheral autonomic symptoms (tremor, tachycardia) without affecting cognition; CBT is first-line for longer-term/generalised social anxiety (eTG Psychotropic; AMH).
Benzodiazepines impair fine motor performance and cognition; not preferred where sensorimotor task required. Would be correct only in non-motor performance with high distress (Source: AMH).

SSRIs are first-line for generalised social anxiety but take 4-6 weeks and can paradoxically worsen anxiety in first 1-2 weeks; not appropriate for single performance. Would be correct in generalised SAD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Quetiapine not indicated for performance anxiety; sedation impairs fine motor control and metabolic effects outweigh benefit. (Source: AMH).
CBD does not have established evidence for performance anxiety in AU; quality control and PBS access limiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Discontinuation syndrome occurs within days of stopping or markedly reducing a serotonergic antidepressant, especially short-half-life agents (paroxetine, venlafaxine). The FINISH mnemonic captures the clinical picture: Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance (brain zaps), Hyperarousal/anxiety. Distinguish from relapse by onset within days, sensory features, and rapid resolution on reinstating the drug.
key_points: Highest risk: paroxetine, venlafaxine (short half-lives); lowest: fluoxetine
FINISH features begin within 1-7 days, peak within 1 week
Restart same drug at previous dose; resolves within 24-72 hours
Taper over weeks (longer for paroxetine, venlafaxine); slower in elderly and long-term users
Distinguish from relapse: relapse takes weeks-months and lacks sensory/flu-like features
explanation.pearls: Counsel every antidepressant patient at initiation that abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal-like symptoms; a planned taper at the time of discontinuation reduces unplanned cessation.

options.rationale: Onset within days of cessation, somatic and sensory features (brain zaps, dizziness) fit discontinuation syndrome not relapse (which takes weeks). Would be correct only if symptoms weeks after cessation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Afebrile, no neck stiffness, no headache, no rash, clear pharmacological explanation. Would be correct with meningism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Mild nausea without vomiting/diarrhoea and normal bloods do not warrant admission, and misses diagnosis. Would be correct only with significant GI illness (Source: RCH CPG).

These FINISH features (Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance/brain zaps, Hyperarousal) within days of stopping a short-half-life serotonergic agent are classic antidepressant discontinuation syndrome; restarting the original drug typically resolves symptoms within 24-72 hours, then slow taper over weeks (eTG Psychotropic; AMH).
No evidence of inadequate treatment response; reinstating previous effective dose is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Melancholic depression is characterised by anhedonia + biological symptoms (early waking, morning-worse mood, weight loss, psychomotor change) + excessive guilt. It is more common in older adults, has a stronger biological substrate, less placebo response, and a relatively better response to TCAs and ECT compared to atypical features. Distinguish from pseudodementia (improves with treatment, no progressive cognitive decline).
key_points: Melancholic specifier: anhedonia + >=3 of distinct mood, AM-worse, EM waking >=2h, marked psychomotor change, weight loss/anorexia, excessive guilt
Atypical specifier: mood reactivity + >=2 of weight gain/appetite increase, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity
Older-adult MDD: lower MMSE may reflect pseudodementia - reassess after treatment
ECT highly effective in melancholic and psychotic depression
Always rule out organic mimics (thyroid, B12, calcium, hypoactive delirium)
explanation.pearls: If MMSE rises by >=2 after successful treatment of depression, the original cognitive decline was likely pseudodementia, not an early dementia.

options.rationale: Treatment response history informs choice but is not part of melancholic specifier criteria. It says nothing about the pattern of his current episode (Source: DSM-5).
These describe atypical features (mood reactivity, increased appetite/weight, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis), the opposite specifier. Would be correct for atypical specifier (Source: DSM-5).
Demographic factors not part of specifier criteria, although melancholic is more common in older adults. Would never be a criterion (Source: DSM-5).

DSM-5 melancholic features require loss of pleasure in nearly all activities (or lack of reactivity to pleasurable stimuli) PLUS at least three of: distinct quality of depressed mood, morning-worse mood, early morning waking >=2 hours, marked psychomotor change, significant weight loss, excessive guilt - all present here (RANZCP CPG; DSM-5).
Suicidal ideation contributes to severity but is not melancholic-specifier feature. Passive ideation occurs across depressive subtypes, so it does not indicate melancholia (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Atypical depression (DSM-5 specifier) = mood reactivity + 2 or more of significant weight gain or appetite increase, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, long-standing interpersonal rejection sensitivity. Historical RCTs (Liebowitz) demonstrated superior response to MAOIs over TCAs in atypical depression. After failure of two adequate SSRI trials, escalation to an MAOI under specialist supervision is a defensible next step, with strict attention to washout periods and dietary restriction.
key_points: Atypical features: mood reactivity + >=2 of weight gain/hyperphagia, hypersomnia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity
MAOIs: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, moclobemide (RIMA - less dietary restriction)
MAOI washouts: 2 weeks from most SSRIs, 5 weeks from fluoxetine, 1+ week from SNRI
Tyramine-rich foods to avoid with irreversible MAOIs: aged cheese, cured meats, fermented soy, broad bean pods, draught beer
Always check for occult bipolarity (atypical depression look-alike in young women)
explanation.pearls: If atypical features are accompanied by hypomanic episodes, the diagnosis is bipolar II and an MAOI is inappropriate without mood stabiliser cover - re-screen carefully before initiation.

options.rationale: Adding TCA to SSRI risks elevated TCA levels (CYP2D6 inhibition) and is not the recommended next step in atypical depression; evidence favours MAOI. Would be correct after MAOI contraindication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Exceeding licensed maximum dose risks QT prolongation without proven benefit; bupropion not registered for depression in AU (only Zyban for smoking cessation). (Source: TGA).

Atypical depression features (mood reactivity, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity) classically respond preferentially to MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) over SSRIs/TCAs; after two failed SSRI trials, escalation under specialist supervision with washout and dietary education is appropriate (eTG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP CPG).

Mirtazapine causes further weight gain and sedation, worsening existing weight gain and hypersomnia; lacks specific evidence for atypical. Would be correct only without weight/sleep concerns (Source: AMH).

T4 augmentation in euthyroid patient has no evidence for atypical features and risks iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis; T3 is the augmentation agent in TRD. Would be correct only with T3 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: BPD is diagnosed when 5 of 9 DSM-5 criteria are met across a longstanding pervasive pattern. Splitting (alternating idealisation and devaluation) is uncommon in primary mood disorders and is the feature in this presentation that best separates BPD from MDD (RANZCP CPG BPD 2012).
key_points: DSM-5 BPD: 5 of 9 criteria including abandonment fears, unstable relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity, recurrent self-harm/suicidal behaviour, affective lability, emptiness, anger, transient stress-related paranoia/dissociation
Splitting is highly suggestive of BPD and rare in primary mood disorders
Self-harm in BPD is typically chronic, low-lethality and interpersonally triggered
Comorbid MDD is common but does not subsume the personality diagnosis
explanation.pearls: When the team starts to feel 'split' (one clinician idealised, another devalued), reflect this back to the team in supervision - it is diagnostic data, not a personnel issue (RANZCP CPG BPD).

options.rationale: Real-time splitting (idealising the current clinician while devaluing the nurse minutes earlier) within a single assessment, combined with collateral history of the same pattern since adolescence, is the most specific feature pointing to BPD over MDD. MDD does not produce splitting; identity-and-relationships instability is core BPD. The pattern's duration since adolescence (DSM-5 onset criterion) and collateral confirmation increase specificity.
Recurrent self-harm is consistent with BPD but not specific (also MDD, adjustment). On its own it does not separate BPD from MDD (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

Crisis pattern in response to relational stressors is consistent with BPD but not specific; many MDD patients present in interpersonal crisis. Crisis presentations after arguments therefore do not separate BPD from MDD (Source: NHMRC).
Emptiness is part of BPD but also reported in chronic depression; alone does not discriminate. It supports BPD but carries less weight than splitting (Source: NHMRC).
Mood reactivity argues AGAINST melancholic MDD but does not distinguish BPD from atypical-features MDD. Reactive mood is therefore compatible with either diagnosis (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: ASPD requires conduct disorder before age 15 PLUS adult disregard for others' rights, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability, recklessness, irresponsibility and lack of remorse. BPD centres on identity disturbance, fear of abandonment, idealisation/devaluation, emptiness and self-harm. Conduct disorder before age 15 is the most reliable distinguishing marker.
key_points: ASPD diagnosis requires age >=18 AND childhood conduct disorder onset before 15
BPD features absent here: emptiness, abandonment fear, splitting, self-harm
Both have high substance use comorbidity
Forensic comorbidity is much higher in ASPD
Treatment options are limited; psychological interventions modest, no medication for the core disorder
explanation.pearls: Always ask about pre-15 behaviour (truancy, fire-setting, cruelty to animals, theft) when ASPD is on the differential - it is a hard DSM-5 criterion (DSM-5).

options.rationale: Substance use common in both ASPD and BPD; not discriminating. It also lacks the conduct disorder before age 15 that ASPD requires (Source: DSM-5).

Brief unstable relationships occur in both; ASPD ends them out of exploitation/boredom, BPD out of abandonment fear or devaluation, so the reason for ending matters more than the pattern. Without childhood conduct disorder, relationship style alone does not establish ASPD (Source: DSM-5).

DSM-5 ASPD criterion C requires evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15 (criterion A1-15 covers aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness, serious rules violations); his history meets at least three. This is a unique and discriminating criterion - BPD has no childhood-conduct-disorder requirement. Adult callous disregard (criterion 7) further supports.
source_refs: DSM-5-TR ASPD criteria A and C

options.rationale: Irritability is part of both ASPD and BPD criteria; not specific. Would never be discriminating (Source: DSM-5).
Glibness/superficial charm is in Hare's PCL-R psychopathy construct but not DSM-5 ASPD criterion; raises probability but not most specific. Would be specific only in PCL-R framework (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Narcissistic personality disorder is a Cluster B personality disorder featuring grandiosity, need for admiration, sense of entitlement, exploitativeness, lack of empathy, and rage at perceived criticism. It is distinct from BPD (abandonment, emptiness) and ASPD (early conduct disorder, criminality).
key_points: NPD: grandiosity + need for admiration + lack of empathy across multiple contexts
Onset by early adulthood, stable over time
Often presents at crisis points (relationship breakdown, professional setback)
No specific pharmacotherapy; psychological therapy can be modestly helpful
explanation.pearls: NPD is often noticed by the team feeling devalued or treated as servants - countertransference is diagnostic data (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Histrionic PD has dramatic, sexually provocative or shallow-affect attention-seeking; he is grandiose and contemptuous rather than dramatic/seductive. Would be correct in dramatic/seductive presentation (Source: DSM-5).

BPD requires identity disturbance, abandonment fear, splitting and impulsive self-damage - all absent. Sustained competent functioning is not BPD pattern. Would be correct in unstable identity/relationships pattern (Source: DSM-5).

ASPD requires childhood conduct disorder (criterion C) and adult pattern of disregard for others' rights/laws; no childhood conduct history, no criminal pattern. Would be correct with conduct disorder before 15 (Source: DSM-5).

NPD meets >=5 of 9 criteria here: grandiose self-importance, fantasies of unlimited brilliance, belief he is 'special', requires excessive admiration, sense of entitlement, interpersonally exploitative, lacks empathy, envious or believes others envy him, arrogant/haughty. Differentiation from ASPD turns on absence of childhood conduct disorder and criminal behaviour; differentiation from histrionic turns on grandiosity vs dramatic emotionality.

OCPD has rigid perfectionism, preoccupation with rules/lists, miserliness, over-conscientiousness; he shows grandiosity and contempt, not perfectionism. Would be correct in perfectionist pattern (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: OCPD behaviours are ego-syntonic and pervasive across life domains; OCD obsessions are intrusive, unwanted and ego-dystonic, with anxiety-driven compulsions performed to reduce distress. Ego-syntonicity is the cleanest line in clinical practice.
key_points: OCPD: 4+ of preoccupation with detail/rules, perfectionism interfering with completion, workaholism, rigid morality, hoarding, reluctance to delegate, miserliness, rigidity/stubbornness
OCD: obsessions + compulsions, distressing and time-consuming
Insight is typically better in OCPD because the person doesn't see the problem
OCD responds to SSRIs + CBT with exposure-response prevention; OCPD does not have a specific treatment
explanation.pearls: If the patient is not distressed by their own behaviour, consider OCPD before OCD (RANZCP anxiety guidance).

options.rationale: Order and control feature in both OCPD and the symmetry/ordering subtype of OCD, so on their own they do not separate the two (Source: DSM-5).

Hoarding can occur in OCPD, hoarding disorder and occasionally OCD; without ego-syntonic/dystonic context does not discriminate. How he experiences the behaviour is more informative than the behaviour itself (Source: DSM-5).

Reluctance to delegate is OCPD criterion but can arise from anxiety in OCD; supportive not decisive. Whether the reluctance comes from perfectionism or from anxiety decides which disorder it supports (Source: DSM-5).
High productivity may occur in either OCPD or unaffected high-functioning workers; not DSM-5 criterion in isolation. Work output does not separate OCPD from OCD (Source: DSM-5).

OCPD behaviours are ego-syntonic - the patient sees them as correct standards and does not experience the intrusive obsessions or anxiety-driven compulsions of ego-dystonic OCD; this is the defining clinical distinction (DSM-5).

explanation.summary: For chronic low-lethality self-harm in BPD with adequate supports, the evidence-based response is a structured safety plan and rapid return to outpatient psychological therapy. Prolonged or routine admissions can worsen outcomes and erode autonomy; involuntary care requires least-restrictive justification.
key_points: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown structure): warning signs, internal coping, social distraction, people to ask for help, professionals/crisis lines, means restriction
Means restriction is a high-yield intervention - handover of medications, removal of access to lethal means
Admission reserved for: acute change in pattern, high-lethality attempt, intent without supports
Comorbidities (MDD, substance use) may shift the threshold for admission
Document risk reasoning explicitly, including least-restrictive justification
explanation.pearls: Chronic vs acute-on-chronic risk: the threshold for admission rises when the pattern is chronic and low-lethality and falls when intent, lethality or means change suddenly (NHMRC BPD).

options.rationale: For low-lethality chronic self-harm in BPD with adequate community supports, NHMRC and RANZCP recommend a structured safety plan (means restriction, identified supports, crisis numbers, early follow-up) and rapid return to the patient's usual psychological therapy; admission is not required when risk can be managed less restrictively (NHMRC BPD; LifeSpan/Black Dog safety planning).

Routine short admissions for chronic low-lethality self-harm in BPD are not recommended; NHMRC favours community management with brief admissions only when essential. Would be correct only for safety crisis not manageable in community (Source: NHMRC BPD).

Involuntary admission requires mental illness plus risk not manageable less restrictively; she has engaged voluntarily with safety plan and trusted clinician. Would never be correct in this scenario (Source: Mental Health Act).
Pharmacotherapy not recommended for core BPD; antipsychotic at discharge after low-lethality overdose adds metabolic risk without benefit. (Source: NHMRC).
AU DBT is predominantly outpatient/day-program; inpatient DBT is not standard; her existing outpatient clinician should continue care. Would never be correct as standard (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Delirium is a clinical diagnosis using the CAM: acute onset and fluctuation PLUS inattention PLUS disorganised thinking OR altered level of consciousness. MMSE/MoCA/GCS are supportive but not delirium-specific. Search for precipitants - infection, hypoxia, medications, electrolytes, pain, constipation, urinary retention.
key_points: CAM = positive when 1+2 AND (3 OR 4)
Inattention is the most discriminating feature (test with backward counting, days of week reverse, serial 7s)
Hyperactive delirium: agitation, restlessness, hallucinations - most easily noticed
Hypoactive delirium: quiet withdrawal, drowsiness - frequently missed
Always reassess in older inpatients each shift
explanation.pearls: If the family says 'this is not how she normally is', screen for delirium with CAM before attributing behaviour to dementia (ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

options.rationale: MMSE detects cognitive impairment but cannot confirm delirium (does not capture acute onset, fluctuation or attentional disturbance specifically). Would be correct only as part of broader CAM-based assessment (Source: ACSQHC).

The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) is positive when there is (1) acute onset and fluctuation AND (2) inattention AND either (3) disorganised thinking OR (4) altered level of consciousness; all four features are present here, confirming delirium (ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard; Inouye CAM).
MoCA detects MCI better than MMSE but does not specifically diagnose delirium (no acute onset/fluctuation capture). Would never alone confirm delirium (Source: ACSQHC).

GCS measures consciousness and is insensitive to attentional and thinking disturbance characterising hyperactive delirium with normal arousal. Would be correct only for impaired conscious level (Source: ACSQHC).
GDS screens for depression in older adults; depression can mimic delirium but is not diagnosed by fluctuating attentional picture. Would be correct only for depression (Source: ACSQHC).

explanation.summary: Hypoactive delirium is the most missed delirium subtype and is often mislabelled as depression. CAM features (acute onset, fluctuating attention, disorganised thinking or altered consciousness) point to delirium. Management is to identify and reverse precipitants - the PINCH-ME mnemonic (Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment) is useful.
key_points: Hypoactive delirium > hyperactive in prevalence and is associated with worse outcomes
Antidepressants do not treat delirium and may worsen confusion, hyponatraemia or anticholinergic burden
Common precipitants: opioids, anticholinergics, infection, electrolytes, urinary retention, constipation
Antipsychotics: lowest effective dose, only when distress or risk; never for hypoactive presentations routinely
Mortality and length of stay rise with delirium - prevention and early reversal are core geriatric care
explanation.pearls: Quiet withdrawn older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise, not depression (ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

options.rationale: Acute onset, fluctuating attention and disorganised thinking is hypoactive delirium not depression; starting antidepressant first misses underlying medical cause. Would be correct in confirmed depression (Source: ACSQHC).

Antipsychotics are reserved for delirium with severe agitation or distress risking harm; hypoactive presentations should not be routinely treated with antipsychotics. Would be correct only with severe agitation (Source: ACSQHC).

The CAM features are met for hypoactive delirium. The single most appropriate step is to identify and reverse precipitants: stop the newly added opioid, correct hyponatraemia with judicious fluid management, ensure ongoing UTI treatment, optimise environment, hydration, mobilisation and orientation (ACSQHC Delirium CCS).

CT brain is for delirium with focal neurology, head injury, anticoagulation or unexplained drop in conscious level; routine imaging not first-line. Would be correct only with focal features (Source: ACSQHC).
ECT not first-line in this acute medical context; diagnosis is not depression and ECT is for severe treatment-resistant or psychotic depression. Would never be correct in delirium (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Onset and course are the most reliable clinical features in distinguishing dementia (gradual, progressive, stable attention) from delirium (acute, fluctuating, impaired attention) and from depressive pseudodementia (subacute, mood-driven, often complaints of cognitive failure with effortful but accurate testing). Investigations help exclude reversible causes.
key_points: Dementia: gradual, months-years, attention typically preserved early
Delirium: acute, fluctuating, attention markedly impaired
Depression: subacute, mood symptoms primary, complains of memory more than tested
Dementia workup: FBC, EUC, LFT, TFT, B12/folate, Ca, glucose, MSU, CT or MRI
Mixed presentations are common - re-screen after delirium resolution
explanation.pearls: Anchor on the family timeline: 'When was he last himself?' - gradual months means dementia, hours-to-days means delirium (Dementia Australia).

options.rationale: Preserved interest argues against major depression but does not distinguish dementia from delirium; delirium can have preserved interest. Preserved interest therefore leaves delirium open (Source: Dementia Australia).

Low MMSE shows cognitive impairment but cannot distinguish delirium from dementia or depression-related cognitive impairment alone. Impaired recall can occur in all three conditions (Source: Dementia Australia).

Cortical atrophy on CT is common in older adults and supports neurodegeneration but is non-specific; does not distinguish from delirium in comorbid case. The time course of decline carries more weight than the imaging (Source: RANZCR).

Dementia typically progresses gradually over months to years without acute onset or marked diurnal fluctuation in attention, distinguishing it from delirium and from pseudodementia of severe depression; this temporal profile is the most useful single feature (Dementia Australia clinical resources; RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide; RANZCP).

Getting lost is suggestive but can occur in delirium with disorientation; temporal profile is more diagnostic than single deficit. Disorientation of this kind does not by itself exclude delirium (Source: Dementia Australia).

explanation.summary: BPSD is a final common pathway with many drivers. First-line care is to look for and treat unmet needs (pain, infection, constipation, urinary retention, hunger, fatigue, sensory deficits, environmental triggers) and apply non-pharmacological strategies (routine, meaningful activity, family contact, orientation, music). Antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress or risk after non-pharmacological measures.
key_points: Pain is often missed in advanced dementia - use Abbey Pain Scale and trial scheduled analgesia
Late-afternoon agitation (sundowning) responds to light, routine, reduced demands
Antipsychotics in dementia: increased stroke and mortality - use lowest dose for shortest time
Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls
Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine have only modest BPSD effects
explanation.pearls: If a person with dementia 'changes', screen for pain, infection, constipation and urinary retention before reaching for an antipsychotic (Dementia Australia BPSD).

options.rationale: Antipsychotics in BPSD are for severe distress or risk of harm not responsive to non-pharmacological measures; this patient has treatable pain, and antipsychotics should follow first-line measures. Would be correct only after first-line failure with severe distress (Source: AMH).
Benzodiazepines worsen confusion, falls and fracture risk in older adults with dementia; not first-line for BPSD. (Source: AMH).
Donepezil not licensed at 23 mg in Australia; dose escalation is not first response to BPSD. Would never be correct in AU (Source: AMH; TGA).

SSRIs (especially citalopram) have modest BPSD evidence but should follow non-pharmacological measures; citalopram over 20 mg in older adults raises QT risk. Would be correct only after first-line failure (Source: AMH).

First-line BPSD management is non-pharmacological with attention to unmet needs - pain, infection, constipation, hunger, fatigue, environment and meaningful activity; a likely pain contributor warrants scheduled analgesia plus orientation, family contact, predictable routine and meaningful engagement (Dementia Australia BPSD; RACGP).

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics in dementia carry an increased risk of stroke and all-cause mortality. Use is restricted to severe BPSD with significant distress or risk after non-pharmacological measures, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, with mandatory review and deprescribing attempt within 12 weeks. Risperidone holds the only Australian indication.
key_points: Risperidone: 0.25-1 mg BD short-term for severe BPSD
Mandatory 12-week review and deprescribing attempt
Increased stroke and mortality in dementia is a class effect
Avoid haloperidol unless severe delirium and short-term
Avoid benzodiazepines for BPSD
explanation.pearls: If an antipsychotic is started for BPSD, put the deprescribing review on the diary the same day - not at 12 months (Dementia Australia BPSD; AMH).

options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic with a specific Australian indication for short-term treatment of severe BPSD; recommended dose is low (0.25-1 mg BD) with mandatory review at no more than 12 weeks because of stroke and mortality risk (AMH; Dementia Australia BPSD; TGA risperidone PI).

Olanzapine 10 mg is standard adult dose, not low-dose-elderly; indefinite continuation is contrary to guideline to review and deprescribe at 12 weeks. Would be correct only at lower dose with scheduled review (Source: AMH).

Haloperidol has higher EPSE and QT risk in older adults; not first-line for BPSD, reserved for short-term severe delirium-related agitation. Would be correct only in short-term severe agitation (Source: AMH).

Quetiapine has weaker evidence in BPSD outside Parkinson dementia/DLB, and 100 mg BD exceeds cautious starting dose in older adults. Would be correct only at lower dose for DLB/Parkinson dementia (Source: AMH).
Benzodiazepines worsen confusion, gait, falls and pneumonia risk in older adults; not appropriate for psychotic features. (Source: Choosing Wisely).

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia and is characterised by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and Parkinsonism. Patients have marked neuroleptic sensitivity - antipsychotics (especially typicals and risperidone) can cause severe deterioration. Cholinesterase inhibitors are preferred for neuropsychiatric symptoms.
key_points: DLB core features: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, Parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder
Avoid haloperidol and conventional antipsychotics; prefer quetiapine if antipsychotic essential
Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) - improve cognition and hallucinations
Levodopa can worsen hallucinations - weigh against Parkinsonism gain
Falls are common - review hypotension, deprescribe sedatives
explanation.pearls: Visual hallucinations + Parkinsonism + fluctuation in an older adult is DLB until proven otherwise - do not give haloperidol (Dementia Australia).

options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics including haloperidol can produce severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions in DLB (worsening Parkinsonism, severe sedation, autonomic instability). Would never be correct in DLB (Source: RANZCP).

Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine and donepezil) have evidence for cognition, fluctuation and visual hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies and are recommended first-line for neuropsychiatric symptoms over antipsychotics, given the neuroleptic sensitivity of DLB (AMH; Dementia Australia; RANZCP).

Risperidone is licensed for BPSD generally but should be avoided in DLB due to severe neuroleptic sensitivity; low-dose quetiapine preferred if any antipsychotic required. Would be correct in non-DLB BPSD (Source: AMH).

Levodopa can worsen visual hallucinations in DLB even though it may improve Parkinsonism; trade-offs must be weighed and not first response to hallucinations. Would be correct only with motor priority (Source: AMH).
Benzodiazepines worsen falls and confusion in DLB and do not treat the underlying neuropsychiatric symptoms. (Source: Choosing Wisely).

explanation.summary: Mild cognitive impairment is the bridge between normal age-related cognitive change and dementia: objective cognitive impairment greater than expected for age and education, but preservation of instrumental activities of daily living (managing finances, medications, driving, cooking, shopping). The dementia threshold is crossed when IADL function declines - cognitive screen scores alone (MMSE, MoCA, ACE-III) cannot make this distinction. Annual MCI-to-dementia progression is around 10-15%, but a substantial proportion remain stable or revert to normal with reversible-cause treatment. Australian practice is to screen for and address reversible contributors (vitamin B12, TSH, depression, sleep apnoea, alcohol use, polypharmacy, anticholinergic burden, hearing and vision impairment), optimise vascular risk factors (BP, lipids, diabetes, smoking, exercise), encourage cognitive and social engagement, and monitor annually with cognitive testing and functional history (ideally with collateral from a partner or close family member). Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated in MCI - they are reserved for established dementia.
key_points: MCI vs dementia: function preserved vs significantly impaired
MoCA more sensitive than MMSE for MCI (cut-off ~26)
No medications licensed for MCI in Australia
Exercise, sleep, vascular risk control, cognitive engagement
Annual reassessment with caregiver collateral
explanation.pearls: Mild cognitive impairment is defined by objective cognitive impairment with preserved instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs); the dementia line is set by functional decline, not by cognitive screen scores. About 10-15% of MCI progresses to dementia per year (Dementia Australia; NIA-AA).

options.rationale: Major NCD (dementia) requires significant functional impairment which this man does not have; cholinesterase inhibitors not licensed for MCI. Would be correct only with functional impairment (Source: DSM-5).
Objective cognitive impairment beyond age expectation on MoCA with corroborated functional change excludes normal ageing. (Source: DSM-5).

MCI is defined as objective cognitive decline beyond age expectation with preserved functional independence; recommended management is structured monitoring (typically 6-12 monthly), cardiovascular risk optimisation, lifestyle (exercise, sleep, social engagement) and review for reversible factors (Dementia Australia; RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide).

Vascular dementia requires evidence of cerebrovascular disease and stepwise decline; no infarcts on imaging and gradual course; already on statin. Would be correct with imaging-confirmed cerebrovascular disease (Source: RANZCR).
Subjective cognitive decline applies when complaint exists without objective deficit; MoCA shows objective impairment moving classification to MCI. Would be correct with normal MoCA (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision-specific, time-specific, and presumed unless disproven. The functional test asks whether the person can understand, retain, weigh and communicate the information for the specific decision. Cognitive screening informs but does not determine capacity.
key_points: Functional test: understand, retain, weigh, communicate
Decision-specific - capacity for surgery can co-exist with incapacity for finances
Time-specific - reassess if delirium, intoxication or medication effects change
Diagnosis alone (dementia, mental illness) does not establish incapacity
If incapable: enduring guardian > tribunal-appointed guardian > responsible person under state law > medical practitioner emergency provisions
explanation.pearls: Document capacity assessment in the patient's own words; that record is the strongest medico-legal protection (RACGP).

options.rationale: Capacity is not determined by cognitive test score; MoCA cut-off is for screening cognitive impairment, not capacity. (Source: state Guardianship Acts).
Dementia diagnosis does not equal incapacity; many with mild dementia retain decision-specific capacity. Assumption of incapacity is contrary to AU principles. (Source: Guardianship Acts).
Substitute decision-makers are engaged only when person lacks capacity; defaulting to family bypasses autonomy. Would be correct only after demonstrated lack of capacity (Source: Guardianship Acts).

Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. She can understand, retain, weigh and communicate the information relevant to this decision in her own words; she meets the functional test for capacity for this surgical consent despite mild dementia (Australian Law Reform Commission; RACGP; respective state Guardianship Acts).
MHA does not authorise consent to surgical procedures; for incapable patients without advance directive or guardian, guardianship pathways apply. (Source: MHA).

explanation.summary: Late-life depression is treated with SSRIs as first-line; sertraline is commonly preferred in older adults given safety profile. Start low (often half adult dose), monitor for SIADH (particularly with thiazide co-prescription), falls, GI bleeding and discontinuation. Avoid TCAs and high-dose citalopram in this group.
key_points: First-line late-life depression: SSRI (sertraline commonly preferred)
Start at half the adult dose and titrate slowly
Monitor sodium at 1-2 weeks, especially with thiazide or carbamazepine
SSRI risks in older adults: SIADH, falls, GI bleeding, QT (citalopram)
Avoid TCAs and paroxetine
explanation.pearls: Always check baseline sodium and recheck at 1-2 weeks after starting an SSRI in an older adult on a thiazide (eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

options.rationale: TCAs are avoided in older adults (anticholinergic load: cognition, falls, constipation, urinary retention) and overdose toxicity. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: AMH).
Citalopram doses above 20 mg in older adults not recommended (QT risk); 40 mg as starting dose is contraindicated. Would be correct only at start dose 10 mg (Source: TGA).

Venlafaxine has dose-dependent HTN and discontinuation effects; 150 mg starting dose in older adult with CKD and antihypertensives is too high. Would be correct only at lower starting dose (Source: AMH).
Mirtazapine can be useful when insomnia/weight loss dominate but 45 mg is too high a starting dose in older adult (typical start 15 mg). Would be correct at 15 mg start (Source: AMH).

Sertraline is a preferred SSRI in older adults given low drug-interaction profile, weak QT effect, and broad evidence in late-life depression. Start at half adult dose and monitor for SIADH/hyponatraemia (already 134 with thiazide co-prescription) and for falls/fractures (eTG Psychotropic; AMH; RANZCP Mood Disorders 2020).

explanation.summary: Therapy choice matches the clinical pattern. IPT and CBT lead in perinatal depression. ACT has its strongest evidence in chronic pain and treatment-resistant anxiety. DBT is reserved for BPD/self-harm. EMDR is indicated for PTSD. Psychodynamic therapy is a longer-term option where access permits.
key_points: IPT - perinatal depression, grief, role transitions
ACT - chronic pain, treatment-resistant anxiety, values-based behaviour change
CBT - broad first-line for anxiety, OCD, PTSD (trauma-focused), MDD
DBT - BPD and recurrent self-harm
EMDR - PTSD
Match therapy to formulation, not just diagnosis label
explanation.pearls: If the clinical formulation centres on role transition or interpersonal loss, IPT is often the highest-value match (RANZCP Perinatal).

options.rationale: ACT has growing evidence in perinatal populations but not first-line per COPE for postnatal MDD; reserved as alternative if IPT/CBT unavailable. Would be correct only if first-line unavailable (Source: COPE).

IPT has the strongest postnatal-specific evidence base (multiple RCTs including O'Hara 2000; Stuart manual); the role-transition focus is mechanistically matched to the parenthood transition that triggered her episode. COPE positions IPT and CBT as first-line for postnatal MDD, with IPT specifically called out for role-transition presentations.
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline 2023
O'Hara et al RCT IPT postnatal

options.rationale: Insufficient RCT evidence in postnatal depression; not first-line. Would never be correct as first-line (Source: COPE).
EMDR is for PTSD, not postnatal MDD without trauma history. Would be correct with PTSD (Source: Phoenix Australia).
DBT is for BPD and chronic self-harm, not postnatal MDD. Would be correct in BPD (Source: NHMRC BPD).

explanation.summary: The transtheoretical (Prochaska-DiClemente) stages of change model frames behaviour change as movement through precontemplation (no awareness or intent to change), contemplation (aware, ambivalent), preparation (planning concrete steps within 30 days), action (active change for less than 6 months), and maintenance (sustained change beyond 6 months), with relapse looping back to any earlier stage. Motivational interviewing is the matched intervention for contemplation and early preparation: it elicits the patient's own change talk, works with ambivalence by reflection rather than confrontation, and follows the FRAMES structure (Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu of options, Empathy, Self-efficacy). Common clinician errors include premature problem-solving (moving to action plans before the patient is ready), confrontation, and giving unsolicited advice - all push the patient back into precontemplation. Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder (naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram) is appropriate in action stage with adequate motivation and abstinence goals.
key_points: Precontemplation: not considering change
Contemplation: aware of problem, ambivalent, no firm plan in 30 days
Preparation: plan within 30 days
Action: changes initiated in past 6 months
Maintenance: sustained for >6 months
MI core skills: OARS - Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries
explanation.pearls: In motivational interviewing, sustain talk (the patient arguing against change) is a clinician error - the technique requires rolling with resistance through reflection, not pushing harder. The FRAMES brief intervention is the evidence-based outpatient package: Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu, Empathy, Self-efficacy (eTG Addiction).

options.rationale: Precontemplation = no awareness; he has acknowledged 'might be a bit too much', which is awareness without commitment. That is contemplation. Would be correct only without any acknowledgement (Source: Prochaska/DiClemente).

Preparation requires intention to act within 30 days and concrete planning; he has neither. Jumping to quit date risks engagement loss. Would be correct only with stated intention and planning (Source: Prochaska).

Stage matching: he acknowledges the problem (past precontemplation) but is ambivalent and not yet planning concrete action (not yet preparation). MI is stage-matched. Importantly, stage matching does NOT mean withholding evidence-based pharmacotherapy: AUDIT >=20 and end-organ damage independently justify offering naltrexone or acamprosate now, framed as supports for the change he is contemplating, not as imposed treatments.
Action requires active behaviour change within last 6 months; he has not yet started. Would be correct only after change initiated (Source: Prochaska).
Maintenance follows 6+ months of sustained behaviour change; not applicable. Would be correct only after sustained change (Source: Prochaska).

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant or recurrent depression with prominent interpersonal and self-critical themes is one of the clearest indications for short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy. Choice between CBT, IPT, ACT and psychodynamic approaches is matched to formulation and prior response, not loaded onto a single modality.
key_points: Recurrent depression with relational patterns - consider time-limited psychodynamic
Treatment-resistant anxiety / chronic pain - ACT
BPD / recurrent self-harm - DBT
Perinatal depression / grief - IPT
Primary anxiety disorders / OCD / PTSD - CBT (often trauma-focused for PTSD)
explanation.pearls: When the patient says 'something deeper isn't shifting' after good CBT trials, that is a clinical cue toward a relational-pattern-focused therapy (RANZCP Mood Disorders 2020).

sources.label: Cochrane: Short-term psychodynamic therapy for depression

options.rationale: Two prior CBT courses with partial transient response; repeating same modality without changing formulation unlikely to produce durable change. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).
Supportive counselling is adjunctive but not structured first-line therapy for recurrent depression with relational patterns. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: RANZCP).
DBT is first-line for BPD and recurrent self-harm, not recurrent MDD with relational patterns without personality disorder features. Would be correct in BPD (Source: NHMRC BPD).

Short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy has evidence in recurrent depression with prominent interpersonal patterns and self-criticism, especially in psychologically minded patients who have plateaued on CBT; it explores recurrent relational patterns and unconscious contributors (RANZCP Mood Disorders 2020; Cochrane Short-term Psychodynamic).
source_refs: Cochrane: Short-term psychodynamic therapy for depression

options.rationale: ACT has evidence in chronic pain and treatment-resistant anxiety; reasonable alternative but psychodynamic better matched for recurrent depression with relational patterns. Would be correct as alternative (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: In delirium superimposed on dementia, capacity must be reassessed at the new baseline once the delirium has resolved, before any substitute decision-maker steps in. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; an enduring guardian acts only when capacity is absent for the relevant decision. The least-restrictive principle applies throughout.
key_points: Delirium often unmasks underlying dementia but resolves to baseline once the precipitant is treated
Always reassess capacity at the new baseline before placement decisions
Enduring guardian acts only when capacity is absent for the decision in question
Risk of harm in the community is balanced against autonomy under the least-restrictive principle
If capacity is uncertain, the relevant state guardianship tribunal arbitrates
Document the capacity reasoning in the patient's own words
explanation.pearls: Family wishes do not override capable refusal - they are weighed and discussed, not enacted by default (Australian Law Reform Commission).

options.rationale: Enduring guardians make substitute decisions only when person lacks capacity for that particular decision; if patient has capacity, refusal stands. Would be correct only after capacity assessment confirms incapacity (Source: Guardianship Acts).
MHA addresses mental illness with risk not manageable less restrictively; does not authorise placement decisions for cognitive impairment without mental illness. (Source: MHA).
Discharge requires assessment of safe destination, supports, and (if capacity in question) documented capacity assessment; immediate discharge bypasses this. (Source: ACSQHC).
Infection has resolved; ongoing antibiotics expose to harm without benefit and do not resolve discharge question. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. The delirium has now resolved (CAM negative, returned to baseline cognition); a fresh functional assessment for the specific decision of discharge destination is required before any substitute decision-maker is engaged or any application made to the Civil and Administrative Tribunal of the relevant state (ALRC; RACGP; state Guardianship Acts).

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is the leading driver of the 10-20 year mortality gap in schizophrenia and is preventable with structured monitoring. The RANZCP-endorsed schedule for any patient on a second-generation antipsychotic is: baseline weight, BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose (or HbA1c), and fasting lipid profile; repeat the full panel at 6 weeks, 12 weeks, and annually thereafter. ECG is at baseline and repeated only if clinical change or new QT-prolonging medication; prolactin is checked when symptomatic. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic burden, quetiapine and risperidone are intermediate, aripiprazole and lurasidone are lowest. Intervention triggers are sustained weight gain over 7% from baseline, new HbA1c over 48, fasting glucose over 6.1, LDL over 3.5, or established metabolic syndrome - escalate lifestyle measures, add metformin (off-label), or switch antipsychotic. Waist circumference is the earliest mover and the easiest to track at each visit.
key_points: Baseline: weight, BMI, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, ECG
Follow-up: 6 wk, 12 wk, then annually (more often if abnormal)
Clozapine adds baseline echocardiogram, troponin, CRP
Switch consideration triggered by >7% weight gain or new metabolic syndrome criteria
explanation.pearls: RANZCP metabolic monitoring schedule: baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, then annually - weight, BMI, waist, BP, fasting glucose (or HbA1c) and fasting lipids. Olanzapine has the highest weight-gain and dysglycaemia signal of the SGAs (RANZCP; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.rationale: RANZCP schedule explicitly includes fasting glucose (or HbA1c) and lipids at 12 weeks, plus anthropometry and BP; highest-risk metabolic changes emerge in first 12 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Metabolic Monitoring).

At the 12-week timepoint the schedule mandates full anthropometric panel (weight, BMI, waist), BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and fasting lipids; ECG repetition is not routinely required at 12 weeks unless QTc prolongation risk has changed (new QTc-prolonging drug, electrolyte derangement, syncope). This is the highest-yield repeat-monitoring window because olanzapine-related weight gain and dyslipidaemia peak in the first 3-6 months.
OGTT, fasting insulin and HOMA-IR are not part of routine RANZCP schedule; fasting glucose/HbA1c plus lipids sufficient at 12 weeks. Would be correct only in research protocols (Source: RANZCP).

Not part of metabolic monitoring schedule; prolactin monitored only on prolactin-elevating antipsychotics (risperidone, amisulpride); 24-h ABPM not routine. Would never be correct as a metabolic panel (Source: RANZCP).
Olanzapine carries highest metabolic-burden signal among SGAs; first 12 weeks is when emergent dyslipidaemia and impaired fasting glucose appear. (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Clozapine has the strongest weight-gain and dyslipidaemia signal of any antipsychotic. In a clear responder, the framework is continue + intervene + intensify monitoring, not stop or halve (RANZCP; AMH).
key_points: >7% weight gain at 12 weeks triggers active intervention
Metformin has the strongest evidence among adjuncts for antipsychotic weight gain
Lifestyle + cardiometabolic review are mandatory, not optional
Cessation reserved for treatment failure, agranulocytosis, myocarditis, or refractory metabolic disease despite intervention
explanation.pearls: A 4-6 week reassessment after starting metformin gives an objective signal; aim to keep him on clozapine if at all possible (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Abrupt clozapine cessation in responder without safety crisis risks rapid psychotic relapse and rebound psychosis; metabolic changes are significant but not life-threatening immediately. Would be correct only in life-threatening adverse event (Source: RANZCP).

He has gained >7% body weight (11% in 12 weeks), with new impaired fasting glucose and atherogenic dyslipidaemia. Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic and AMH support continuing clozapine in a clear responder while adding lifestyle support, considering metformin (which has the best evidence for antipsychotic-induced weight gain), and tightening cardiometabolic monitoring; repeat panel at 4-6 weeks tracks response.
11 percent weight gain with new dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia at 12 weeks meets RANZCP threshold for intensified monitoring and active intervention, not deferral. (Source: RANZCP).

Halving effective clozapine risks loss of response; not the recommended first step for metabolic adverse effects (pharmacological and lifestyle adjuncts first). Would never be correct as first step (Source: AMH).

No symptoms or signs of myocarditis (no chest pain, dyspnoea, fever, tachycardia, raised troponin/CRP); urgent echo with cessation is not warranted. Would be correct only with myocarditis features (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Switching antipsychotic for metabolic reasons is a routine outpatient decision when sustained weight gain, dysglycaemia or dyslipidaemia develops despite structured lifestyle intervention and consideration of metformin augmentation (off-label, 1000-2000 mg/day). The lowest metabolic burden in available Australian agents lies with aripiprazole and lurasidone; medium-burden options include risperidone and ziprasidone. Cross-tapering preserves psychiatric stability: introduce the new agent at therapeutic dose over 2-4 weeks while reducing the original over the same period. Existing diabetes therapy (metformin, SGLT2i), antihypertensive, and statin prescriptions are continued unchanged - the underlying disease persists even after the drug-driver is removed. Bariatric surgery is considered for patients with BMI over 35 with comorbidities or over 40 alone, who have psychiatric stability. Document the metabolic rationale clearly to support continuity of care and audit.
key_points: Switch agents: aripiprazole, lurasidone, ziprasidone, brexpiprazole have lowest metabolic burden
Cross-taper rather than abrupt switch to limit relapse risk
Continue diabetes and BP management through the switch
Reassess metabolic profile 6-12 weeks after switch
explanation.pearls: Trigger for switching antipsychotic on metabolic grounds: sustained weight gain over 7% from baseline, new or worsening dysglycaemia, new dyslipidaemia, or metabolic syndrome despite lifestyle and metformin. Cross-taper to aripiprazole or lurasidone, retain metabolic comorbidity treatment (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Topiramate has modest evidence for antipsychotic-induced weight gain and is third-line after lifestyle and metformin; with established T2DM, switching the offending agent is preferred. Would be correct as third-line adjunct (Source: RANZCP).
Dose reduction has only weak effect on weight in established olanzapine-induced metabolic syndrome and risks symptomatic relapse. Would never be correct as primary intervention (Source: RANZCP).
Chlorpromazine is high-burden for weight, sedation, anticholinergic load and adds postural hypotension; not a metabolically favourable switch. (Source: AMH).

She has overt metabolic syndrome with T2DM (HbA1c 7.5%) and >7% sustained weight gain on olanzapine. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic recommend switching to a metabolically lower-burden agent (aripiprazole or lurasidone, both PBS-listed) via cross-taper, with continued antidiabetic and antihypertensive therapy and close monitoring for relapse; she previously tolerated aripiprazole.

Bariatric surgery may have role in selected cases but is not first-line ahead of switching to metabolically favourable antipsychotic; continuing offending drug persists root cause. Would be correct only after failed switch and intensive lifestyle (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L for maintenance, up to 1.0 for acute mania) and is renally cleared, so any factor reducing glomerular filtration or sodium delivery raises plasma lithium toward toxic ranges. The high-yield drug interactions are NSAIDs (reduce renal prostaglandins, lower GFR, raise lithium by 25-60%), ACE inhibitors and ARBs (similar mechanism, raise lithium by 25-30%), thiazides (volume depletion, sodium loss, raise lithium by 25-40%), and metronidazole. Dehydration from diarrhoea, vomiting, fever, exercise, or hot weather is the most common precipitant of community lithium toxicity. Every lithium patient should have a written sick-day plan covering: maintain fluids in heat or illness, avoid NSAIDs (paracetamol is the safe alternative), check level if vomiting or diarrhoea over 24 hours, and the symptoms of early toxicity (tremor worsening, drowsiness, ataxia, diarrhoea). Quarterly lithium level, eGFR, calcium and TSH are standard maintenance monitoring.
key_points: NSAIDs (selective and non-selective) reduce renal lithium clearance
ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce lithium clearance
Thiazides reduce lithium clearance more than loop diuretics
Dehydration (heat, vomiting, diarrhoea) is the commonest precipitant of community lithium toxicity
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance is renal: anything reducing eGFR raises lithium levels. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, and dehydration are the main acute culprits. Paracetamol is the safest analgesic for short-term use in any lithium patient (AMH; NPS MedicineWise).

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH): lithium drug interactions

options.rationale: Non-selective NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance via afferent arteriole prostaglandin effect; combined with ACE inhibitor and thiazide-like risks toxicity. Would be correct only without lithium (Source: AMH).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH): lithium drug interactions

options.rationale: COX-2 selective agents also reduce renal lithium clearance and are not safe substitute when avoiding lithium toxicity. (Source: AMH).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH): lithium drug interactions

options.rationale: Naproxen interacts strongly with lithium; topical diclofenac has some systemic absorption and does not solve interaction. (Source: AMH).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH): lithium drug interactions

options.rationale: Abruptly switching long-stable mood stabiliser for short-term analgesia exposes to relapse and valproate toxicity; not proportionate. (Source: RANZCP).

Paracetamol does not interact with lithium and is the safest analgesic choice. The Australian Medicines Handbook and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic emphasise avoiding NSAIDs, ACE inhibitor changes, and dehydration in patients on lithium, particularly during hot weather; she has a triple-whammy setup (ACEi + thiazide-like diuretic + lithium) and is travelling to hot weather, so hydration advice and a low threshold to recheck levels are essential.
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH): lithium drug interactions

explanation.summary: Lithium neurotoxicity is a clinical syndrome that develops over hours to days as plasma levels rise from therapeutic toward toxic. Early features (level around 1.5-2.0) include worsening tremor, drowsiness, dysarthria, ataxia, fasciculations and nausea. Severe toxicity (level above 2.5) produces frank cerebellar signs (coarse nystagmus, dysarthria, ataxia), hyperreflexia, clonus (but without the autonomic features of serotonin toxicity), confusion, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmia. Importantly, plasma levels lag CNS toxicity in chronic toxicity, where total body lithium is high but plasma is only modestly elevated. The diagnostic clue in an established stable patient is the development of cerebellar signs on a background of years of stable lithium therapy - usually triggered by dehydration, NSAID use, ACE inhibitor introduction, or renal impairment. Management is immediate cessation of lithium, IV crystalloid to restore renal perfusion, and emergency haemodialysis for severe toxicity (level above 4.0, or above 2.5 with neurological features, renal failure or cardiac instability).
key_points: Cerebellar + tremor + hyperreflexia = lithium neurotoxicity until proven otherwise
Precipitants: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics, dehydration, acute kidney injury
Always check lithium level, electrolytes, renal function, ECG
Severe toxicity (level >2.5 mmol/L or refractory neurology) is an indication for haemodialysis
explanation.pearls: Lithium neurotoxicity is identified by cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysarthria, coarse nystagmus) plus hyperreflexia plus rising tremor against a baseline of stable lithium therapy - far more specific than the fever and clonus of NMS or serotonin toxicity, which point elsewhere (AMH; NSW Poisons Information Centre).

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: lithium toxicity

options.rationale: Coarse tremor is key feature but non-specific; combination with cerebellar signs is most specific to lithium neurotoxicity. Would never alone be the most specific (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

The classic neurotoxicity picture is cerebellar (ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus) with hyperreflexia and progression toward confusion, seizures, and coma as levels rise; it is highly specific when occurring alongside a rising lithium level and acute kidney injury, as here (ramipril + dehydration + chronic lithium). Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic and the Australian Medicines Handbook list this constellation as the diagnostic signature of lithium neurotoxicity.
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: lithium toxicity

options.rationale: Fever is not a feature of lithium toxicity and points to NMS, serotonin syndrome, or sepsis; he is afebrile. Would be correct only in NMS/serotonin syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Lead-pipe rigidity and autonomic instability characterise NMS not lithium neurotoxicity; he has no rigidity. Would be correct in NMS (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Clonus and ocular clonus are hallmark of serotonin syndrome, not lithium neurotoxicity. Would be correct in serotonin syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The TGA-mandated valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (PPP) applies to all women of childbearing potential prescribed sodium valproate, regardless of indication (bipolar disorder, epilepsy, migraine). Requirements are: highly effective contraception (LARC strongly preferred - implant, IUS, copper IUD; otherwise sterilisation or dual-method), annual review with a specialist who must sign the risk acknowledgement form, documentation that alternative agents have been considered and unsuitable, and a pre-conception switch plan when pregnancy is desired. For bipolar disorder, alternatives include lithium, lamotrigine, and atypical antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine). The 'only effective option' clause requires a documented switching failure trail. When valproate must continue, prescribe at the lowest effective dose, divide into multiple daily doses to lower peak levels, supplement with 5 mg folic acid daily, and ensure obstetric and neonatal teams are aware in advance.
key_points: Fetal valproate syndrome and neural tube defects in around 10% of exposed pregnancies
Neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30-40% of exposed children
Highly effective contraception (LARC or combined hormonal contraception) is mandatory
Annual specialist review with signed acknowledgement of risks
explanation.pearls: The Australian valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program mandates highly effective contraception (LARC preferred), annual specialist review with signed risk acknowledgement, active consideration of alternatives, and a pre-conception switch plan when pregnancy is desired (TGA; RANZCP).

sources.label: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: AU valproate PPP requires highly effective contraception (LARC or combined hormonal) for ALL females of reproductive potential before/during valproate; no change is non-compliant. (Source: TGA Valproate PPP).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: PPP responsibility sits with prescriber; counselling without ensuring effective contraception and signed acknowledgement does not satisfy framework. (Source: TGA).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: The TGA and RANZCP guidance require that valproate in females of reproductive potential is used only when alternatives are unsuitable, with mandatory highly effective contraception, annual specialist review with signed acknowledgement of risks (fetal valproate syndrome, neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental impairment), and an explicit plan to switch before conception. Active reconsideration of alternatives is part of every review (TGA; RANZCP).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of effective mood stabiliser after recent manic episode risks relapse; safer pathway is overlap switch. (Source: RANZCP).
Teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental risk are dose-related but present at all doses; halving does not satisfy PPP. (Source: TGA).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

explanation.summary: In-utero valproate exposure carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of any commonly used anticonvulsant or mood stabiliser. Major congenital malformations (neural tube defects, congenital heart disease, cleft palate, hypospadias) occur in about 10% of exposed pregnancies versus 2-3% background. Beyond structural defects, 30-40% of exposed children have neurodevelopmental impairment including reduced IQ, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and language delay. Risks are dose-dependent, accelerating above 700 mg/day. Pre-conception switching with overlap is the standard - to lithium, lamotrigine or atypical antipsychotic in bipolar; to lamotrigine, levetiracetam or oxcarbazepine in epilepsy.
