Document the conversation jointly with obstetrics or neurology. Frame the conversation in absolute numbers (1 in 10 major malformation, 1 in 3 neurodevelopmental impairment) rather than relative risk, which patients consistently underweight. The TGA black-box warning and PPP framework underpin this guidance.
key_points: Major malformations: about 10% (vs 2-3% background)
Neurodevelopmental impairment: 30-40% of exposed children
Neural tube defects, cardiac, craniofacial, limb anomalies all over-represented
Plan switch well before conception with overlap to maintain mood
explanation.pearls: Valproate in pregnancy carries about 10% major congenital malformation rate (versus 2-3% background) and 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment rate including autism and ADHD; risks are dose-dependent above 700 mg/day. Frame in absolute numbers, not relative risk (TGA; PRIM&R).

sources.label: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: Valproate major malformation rate is ~10 percent (3-4 times background), not 1 percent. (Source: TGA; AMH).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: Major structural malformations including NTDs arise from first-trimester exposure during organogenesis; neurodevelopmental harm spans pregnancy. (Source: TGA).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: High-dose folate is recommended for women on AEDs but does not eliminate valproate teratogenicity; mitigates not eliminates risk. (Source: TGA).

TGA safety advisories and the Australian Medicines Handbook quote major malformation rates of approximately 10% (versus 2-3% background) and neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30-40% of exposed children. RANZCP recommends preconception switching to a lower-risk mood stabiliser with overlap to protect mood stability; lithium remains an option in many women despite past adverse effects, with specialist input. This is the truthful, action-relevant counselling.
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

options.rationale: Fetal valproate syndrome includes irreversible structural malformations and persistent neurodevelopmental impairment; not reversible. (Source: TGA).
source_refs: TGA: Valproate and risks in pregnancy - safety advisory

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose is the highest case-fatality psychotropic exposure in Australia. The lethal mechanisms are sodium-channel blockade producing QRS widening and ventricular arrhythmias, alpha-blockade causing refractory hypotension, anticholinergic delirium, and central seizures - any of these can develop within 2-6 hours of ingestion. ECG signs include QRS over 100 ms, R-wave over 3 mm in aVR, and an R:S ratio over 0.7 in aVR. Sodium bicarbonate (1-2 mmol/kg bolus repeated to QRS narrowing, target pH 7.45-7.55) reverses sodium-channel blockade. Single-dose activated charcoal is reasonable within an hour of ingestion in a protected airway. Benzodiazepines manage seizures and agitation; intralipid is a salvage option for refractory cardiac toxicity. Flumazenil is contraindicated. Phone the NSW Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) early - they coordinate Australia-wide.
key_points: QRS >100 ms predicts seizures; >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias
R wave aVR >3 mm and terminal R/S aVR >0.7 are sensitive markers
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus, titrate to QRS and pH ~7.50
Benzodiazepines for seizures; avoid flumazenil and class I antiarrhythmics
explanation.pearls: TCA toxicity is driven by sodium-channel blockade; treat any QRS over 100 ms, any ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension with 1-2 mmol/kg IV sodium bicarbonate bolus, targeting serum pH 7.45-7.55 and serum sodium up to 150 (NSW Poisons Information Centre).

options.rationale: Oral charcoal is contraindicated with declining GCS and unprotected airway; observation alone misses urgent indication for bicarbonate. Would be correct only in alert protected airway within 1-2 h (Source: NSW PIC).
Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose (precipitates seizures and arrhythmias by removing GABAergic protection). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Class IA and IC antiarrhythmics worsen sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; bicarbonate is the antidote. (Source: NSW PIC).
Magnesium is for torsades from QT prolongation; in TCA overdose the dominant lethal mechanism is QRS prolongation from sodium channel block. Would be correct in torsades (Source: NSW PIC).

QRS >100 ms (especially >120 ms) in tricyclic overdose predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmias and is the classic indication for sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus (titrated to QRS narrowing and pH ~7.50-7.55). NSW Poisons Information Centre and Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology specify this pathway alongside airway protection and seizure management (benzodiazepines first-line).

explanation.summary: The NSW Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) is the Australian 24/7 toxicology phone service that supports rural and metropolitan clinicians; early consultation is the standard of care for any significant overdose (NSW Poisons Information Centre).
key_points: 13 11 26 covers all of Australia, 24/7, free to caller
Use early - the advice helps with disposition and antidote thresholds
Document the consult ID and recommendations
Retrieval decisions for rural patients are part of the consult
explanation.pearls: Save 13 11 26 on every ED resus phone; it costs nothing to call too early (NSW Poisons Information Centre).

options.rationale: The NSW Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) is the national poisons information service for Australia and provides 24/7 specialist toxicology advice including TCA-specific risk stratification, indications for sodium bicarbonate, intubation, and retrieval. NSW Poisons Information Centre and Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology recommend early case-specific consultation, particularly for rural ED clinicians managing infrequent toxidromes; the advice is then documented and acted on.
Waiting for email response delays time-critical decisions; toxicology advice is immediately available by phone. (Source: NSW PIC).
General reference apps may not reflect AU-specific advice; clinician-to-toxicologist captures case nuances apps cannot. Would never be correct as definitive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Discharge of any symptomatic TCA ingestion is not appropriate; QRS can progress, dose is uncertain, minimum 6-h observation with serial ECGs is standard. (Source: NSW PIC).

Intralipid is for refractory cardiovascular collapse from local anaesthetic or some lipophilic drug toxicities; not first-line in stable TCA. Would be correct only in refractory collapse (Source: NSW PIC).

explanation.summary: Clozapine carries a roughly 0.8% lifetime risk of agranulocytosis, peaking in the first 18 weeks, which is why Australia mandates registry enrolment (CPMS, ClopineCentral) and protocolled FBC monitoring lifelong. The green-amber-red zone system uses absolute neutrophil count thresholds of 2.0 and 1.5 x 10^9/L. Amber zone requires the same daily clozapine dose but FBC twice weekly and registry notification; benign ethnic neutropenia (common in patients of African or Middle Eastern descent) gets lower threshold rules through the registry. Red zone means immediate cessation, daily FBC, haematology involvement, and registry-coordinated decision about rechallenge - which is generally prohibited once a true agranulocytosis (under 0.5) has occurred. Other monitoring beyond FBC includes weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks (myocarditis), 6-monthly metabolic profile, and annual ECG.
key_points: Weekly haematological monitoring for 18 weeks, then 4-weekly thereafter
Amber zone (1.5-1.99): continue, weekly bloods until green
Red zone (<1.5): stop clozapine, urgent specialist review
Benign ethnic neutropenia and BEN-modified thresholds may apply with haematology input
explanation.pearls: In Australian clozapine monitoring, an amber-zone ANC (1.5-1.99 x 10^9/L) is continued at full dose with twice-weekly FBC until it returns to green; red-zone (under 1.5) mandates immediate cessation, haematology referral and registry notification (AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.rationale: ANC 1.6 is below AU green-zone threshold (>=2.0) and triggers amber-zone management. (Source: ClopineCentral Australia).

ANC 1.6 falls within the standard Australian amber zone (1.5 to <2.0); the appropriate response is to continue clozapine, increase FBC frequency to at least twice weekly until the count recovers to green, and notify the registry. There is no fever, sore throat or other sepsis flag mandating immediate clozapine cessation, and amber-zone management is well-established to avoid premature loss of a uniquely effective drug in TRS.
ANC 1.6 is amber, not red; immediate cessation is wrong threshold and would unnecessarily strip a TRS patient of effective drug. Would be correct only at ANC under 1.5 (Source: ClopineCentral).
Any drop below green requires accelerated monitoring; routine 4-weekly is unsafe at ANC 1.6 (progression to red zone risk). (Source: ClopineCentral).
Lithium augmentation to raise ANC is not standard of care; correct response is frequent monitoring per registry. Would never be correct as primary response (Source: ClopineCentral).

explanation.summary: Clozapine is metabolised principally by CYP1A2, an enzyme strongly induced by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke (not by nicotine itself). Australian smokers on stable clozapine doses typically have lower troughs than non-smokers on the same milligram dose, and abrupt cessation - common during hospital admissions and in smoke-free mental health units - removes the induction over 1-2 weeks and raises plasma levels by half or more. Untreated, this produces sedation, hypersalivation, postural drop, seizures and a rising QTc. Pre-emptive management for any planned smoke-free admission is a 25-30% clozapine dose reduction with a level at day 5-7 and weekly thereafter until stable. Resumption of smoking on discharge runs the same pharmacokinetic shift in reverse - dose increases are needed within 2 weeks or the patient becomes subtherapeutic.
key_points: PAHs in smoke (not nicotine) drive CYP1A2 induction
Cessation = level rise; resumption = level fall
Plan a dose review and clozapine level on day 7-14 of cessation
Same pharmacokinetic shift applies to olanzapine, theophylline, ropinirole
explanation.pearls: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke (not nicotine) induce CYP1A2, the main clozapine metaboliser; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels by 50-70% over 1-2 weeks, so cut the dose by about 25% on admission and recheck the level at 5-7 days (AMH).

options.rationale: Wrong enzyme and wrong direction. Clozapine is metabolised primarily by CYP1A2 (CYP3A4 minor); PAHs in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2. (Source: AMH).
Nicotine is NOT the CYP1A2 inducer (PAHs are); NRT replaces nicotine for craving control but does not replace PAH-mediated enzyme induction. (Source: AMH).

Mechanism: PAHs (not nicotine) induce CYP1A2 in heavy smokers; on cessation, induction reverses with a half-life of ~1 week, so clozapine clearance falls and levels can rise 50-70 percent. For a 5-day forced abstinence with planned return to smoking, monitor toxicity and check a level. For sustained cessation, a pre-emptive ~25 percent dose reduction with serial levels is recommended (RANZCP and AMH).
Direction reversed: smoking INDUCES CYP1A2 (does not inhibit); cessation raises levels. (Source: AMH).
False; this interaction is one of the most clinically important PAH-CYP1A2 interactions in psychiatry, with documented clozapine toxicity from quitting smoking. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: SSRI-induced syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is a common and under-recognised cause of hyponatraemia in older Australians, occurring in around 5% of older patients started on an SSRI. Risk factors are age over 65, female sex, low body weight, concurrent thiazide diuretic, and the first 2-4 weeks of therapy. Presentation is non-specific: lethargy, falls, gait unsteadiness, anorexia, nausea, headache, and at lower sodiums confusion, seizures and coma. Diagnosis requires euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia (serum osmolality under 275 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium over 30 mmol/L) with exclusion of hypothyroidism and Addison's. Management is cessation of the SSRI and any potentiating drugs (thiazide, carbamazepine), fluid restriction to 800-1000 mL/day, and slow sodium correction (no more than 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination). Hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia. After resolution, an alternative antidepressant with lower SIADH risk (mirtazapine, agomelatine, vortioxetine) can be tried.
key_points: Check sodium at baseline and 2-4 weeks in older patients starting an SSRI
Stop SSRI + offender (thiazide), fluid restrict, controlled correction
Do not correct sodium faster than 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours
Mirtazapine has the lowest hyponatraemia signal among antidepressants
explanation.pearls: SSRI-induced SIADH presents within 2-4 weeks of starting in elderly women, especially when potentiated by concurrent thiazide and low body weight; check sodium in any older patient with falls, lethargy or confusion within a month of starting an SSRI (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - SSRI adverse effects

options.rationale: Thiazide contributes (and should be stopped) but temporal link (12 days after sertraline start) with euvolaemic biochemical SIADH pattern implicates SSRI. Would be correct only without temporal SSRI link (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - SSRI adverse effects

options.rationale: Fluid intake is modest; biochemistry (urine osmolality 412 with serum osmolality 254 and urine Na 48) fits SIADH not primary polydipsia (which would have low urine osmolality). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - SSRI adverse effects

options.rationale: No hypotension, hyperkalaemia, hyperpigmentation or Addisonian features; aggressive saline could cause rapid correction and central pontine myelinolysis. Would be correct only with Addisonian features (Source: APEG).
CSW requires hypovolaemia and is usually after acute neuro injury; she is euvolaemic with no neuro insult. Would be correct in post-neurosurgical setting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

The biochemistry (low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, urine sodium >30 mmol/L, euvolaemia, normal TSH/cortisol pattern, recent SSRI start, concurrent thiazide) is classical SSRI-induced SIADH potentiated by thiazide. Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic and the Australian Medicines Handbook advise stopping the SSRI and the thiazide, fluid restriction, controlled correction (not >8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination), and switching to an antidepressant with lower hyponatraemia risk such as mirtazapine.
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - SSRI adverse effects

explanation.summary: Two key Australian safety items combine here: the TGA citalopram dose cap of 20 mg in adults over 65 (driven by dose-dependent QT prolongation), and the serotonin syndrome triad of mental status change, neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia), and autonomic hyperactivity (TGA; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; AMH).
key_points: Citalopram max in adults over 65: 20 mg daily (TGA QT advisory)
Serotonin syndrome: clonus (especially ocular and inducible/lower-limb), hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds; NO rigidity
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, very high CK; slower onset; antipsychotic trigger
Tramadol is a frequent co-trigger via serotonergic activity
Management: stop offenders, benzodiazepines, cooling, IV fluids, NSW Poisons Information Centre consult, cyproheptadine if refractory
explanation.pearls: Lower-limb-predominant clonus with normal tone is the textbook serotonin-syndrome physical sign; lead-pipe rigidity points the other way to NMS (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

sources.label: TGA: Citalopram and QT prolongation - safety advisory
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - neuroleptic malignant syndrome

options.rationale: His features (clonus, especially inducible and spontaneous lower-limb ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, diaphoresis, fever, lower-limb predominance, NO rigidity) meet Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome. The trigger is the 40 mg citalopram dose (which exceeds the TGA over-65 cap of 20 mg due to dose-dependent QT prolongation and is reflected here in QTc 502 ms) combined with newly added tramadol (serotonergic). Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, the AMH, and the NSW Poisons Information Centre recommend stopping serotonergic agents, benzodiazepine sedation, cooling, IV fluids, ECG/CK monitoring, and cyproheptadine for refractory cases.
source_refs: TGA: Citalopram and QT prolongation - safety advisory

options.rationale: NMS has lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, very high CK (often over 1000), slower onset; no rigidity here. Would be correct in NMS phenotype (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - neuroleptic malignant syndrome

options.rationale: Lactate mildly raised and no clear source; focal clonus and ocular clonus point strongly to serotonin syndrome. Would be correct with documented infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Anticholinergic toxidrome has dry skin/mucosae, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds; he is diaphoretic with hyperactive bowels. Would be correct in anticholinergic pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
No focal neurological deficits; symmetric clonus, fever and autonomic features are not stroke. Thrombolysis would be wholly inappropriate. (Source: ANSCS).

explanation.summary: Eight months of attenuated symptoms followed by persistent third-person auditory hallucinations and delusions, despite four weeks of abstinence and a negative urine screen, is a typical first-episode psychosis presentation. Australian early-psychosis services deliver assertive, multidisciplinary care that shortens duration of untreated psychosis and improves functional outcomes (Source: Orygen EPPIC Model of Care).
key_points: Duration of untreated psychosis is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor (Orygen EPPIC).
Substance-induced psychosis typically resolves within 1 month of abstinence (RANZCP CPG 2016).
Least-restrictive principle governs decisions about involuntary admission under state MHAs (NSW MHA 2007).
explanation.pearls: Negative urine drug screen plus symptoms persisting beyond 4 weeks of abstinence argues against a primary substance-induced psychotic disorder.

options.rationale: Initiating antipsychotic without specialist assessment and formal early-intervention plan is below AU standard of care for FEP; specialist team needed. (Source: EPPIC; RANZCP).

Australian guidance prioritises specialist early-psychosis services with multidisciplinary outreach, low-dose second-generation antipsychotic, psychological therapy and family work to shorten duration of untreated psychosis, which is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor (Source: Orygen EPPIC Model of Care; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).

Symptoms persist 4 weeks after last cannabis use with negative urine screen, exceeding typical resolution for substance-induced psychosis. Would be correct only with shorter symptom course (Source: DSM-5).
Routine neuroimaging and EEG are not required prior to treatment in young adult with typical FEP, normal neurology and normal screen. Would be correct only with focal neuro signs (Source: RANZCP).
Involuntary admission requires risk not manageable less restrictively; engaged with family, denies SI/HI, willing to accept treatment. (Source: MHA).

explanation.summary: Choice of maintenance antipsychotic in young Australian men with first or second episode schizophrenia hinges on adherence and long-term physical health: weight gain, dyslipidaemia, diabetes and hyperprolactinaemia drive both treatment discontinuation and the 10-20 year mortality gap in schizophrenia. Aripiprazole is a partial dopamine D2 agonist with a much flatter metabolic profile than olanzapine, clozapine, quetiapine or risperidone, and it has neutral or lowering effects on prolactin. The trade-offs are akathisia (often dose-related, settles with dose reduction or short-course propranolol) and weaker sedation, which can be a feature or a bug. Long-acting injectable aripiprazole monthly is funded on PBS for relapse prevention and dramatically improves adherence. Baseline and routine metabolic monitoring (weight, BP, fasting lipids, glucose or HbA1c) is mandated for every patient on any antipsychotic.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine: highest metabolic burden.
Risperidone and amisulpride: highest prolactin elevation.
Aripiprazole: metabolically neutral, partial D2 agonist.
Clozapine reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials.
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden of the second-generation antipsychotics: typical weight gain under 1 kg at 12 months versus 4-7 kg with olanzapine or risperidone, and minimal effect on fasting glucose, lipids or prolactin (eTG Psychotropic).

options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the most favourable metabolic profile among second-generation antipsychotics, with minimal weight, glucose, lipid or prolactin effects, and is the preferred switch when metabolic burden and adherence are the limiting factors (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Antipsychotic choice; AMH 2024).

Risperidone causes intermediate weight gain and highest prolactin elevation of common atypicals, with sexual dysfunction and gynaecomastia that often drive non-adherence. Would be correct only without metabolic concerns (Source: AMH).
Quetiapine is highly sedating with significant weight and metabolic risk; short half-life and high doses for antipsychotic efficacy. Would be correct only when sedation desired (Source: AMH).

Amisulpride is effective and metabolically neutral but causes marked hyperprolactinaemia and is renally excreted; sedation and metabolic burden criteria favour aripiprazole. Would be correct in alternative settings (Source: AMH).
Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failure of at least 2 adequate trials; patient has not had 2 trials. Would be correct only in TRS (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Acute dystonic reactions occur in around 5% of patients started on high-potency typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) and a smaller proportion of those on risperidone or aripiprazole. Onset is usually within 5 days of starting or dose increase, often within 24 hours. Risk factors are young age, male sex, antipsychotic-naive status, high-potency D2 blockade, IM route, and rapid dose escalation. Presentation includes sustained torticollis, oculogyric crisis (forced upward gaze), trismus, jaw clenching, opisthotonos and - life-threateningly - laryngeal dystonia with stridor. First-line treatment is parenteral anticholinergic: benzatropine 1-2 mg IM or IV (repeatable at 20 minutes), or diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IM or IV. Symptoms resolve within 5-20 minutes. After acute treatment, reduce the offending antipsychotic dose, switch to a lower-potency agent, or add oral anticholinergic for 24-72 hours.
key_points: Acute dystonia: hours to days after antipsychotic; treat with IM benzatropine 1 to 2 mg.
Akathisia: subjective restlessness; treat by reducing dose, then propranolol or benzodiazepine.
Tardive dyskinesia: months to years; consider VMAT2 inhibitor and clozapine switch.
NMS: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered sensorium.
explanation.pearls: Acute dystonia from high-potency D2 blockade typically appears within 5 days of starting (often within 24 hours); IM benzatropine 1-2 mg or IM diphenhydramine 25-50 mg resolves symptoms within 20 minutes. Young men and naive patients are highest-risk (eTG Psychotropic).

options.rationale: Acute dystonic reaction to high-potency D2 blockade responds rapidly to parenteral anticholinergic; benzatropine 1 to 2 mg IM is first-line in Australian practice and onset is within 15 to 20 minutes (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Movement disorders due to antipsychotics; AMH 2024).

Benzodiazepines are second-line and slower onset; oral absorption is unreliable with oromandibular dystonia; definitive parenteral anticholinergic preferred. Would be correct only when anticholinergic contraindicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Propranolol treats akathisia not acute dystonia; akathisia is restless inability to sit still vs sustained muscle contractions. Would be correct in akathisia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Dantrolene with cooling is NMS management (hyperthermia, generalised rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness). Would be correct in NMS (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Cessation alone does not abort established dystonia (persists hours to days); targeted anticholinergic is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Subjective restlessness with observable pacing days after starting risperidone is akathisia. Australian first-line management is to reduce the dose if possible and add propranolol; emerging suicidal ideation linked to akathisia is a recognised hazard requiring prompt action (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
key_points: Distinguish akathisia (subjective restlessness) from dystonia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia.
First-line: dose reduction plus propranolol.
Second-line: benzodiazepine (short course) or mirtazapine.
Akathisia is associated with suicide risk - never dismiss as 'anxiety'.

options.rationale: Anticholinergics are effective for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism but only modest benefit in akathisia; may worsen cognition and cause urinary retention. Would be correct in dystonia/parkinsonism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Akathisia is best managed by reducing the offending agent where possible and adding a lipid-soluble beta-blocker; propranolol 30 to 80 mg daily in divided doses is the standard Australian first-line pharmacological treatment (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).
Lithium does not treat akathisia; higher level increases tremor, nephrotoxicity and toxicity risk; mania is responding. (Source: AMH).
Clozapine is for TRS after failure of two adequate trials; not appropriate for first antipsychotic side effect. Would be correct only in TRS (Source: RANZCP).
Untreated akathisia is strongly associated with suicidal ideation and non-adherence; expectant management is unsafe. (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: The discriminating neurological signs are lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia (NMS) versus hyperreflexia and inducible/spontaneous clonus (serotonin toxicity); the medication trigger is a D2 antagonist for NMS and a serotonergic drug for serotonin syndrome (Source: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; eTG Psychotropic).
key_points: NMS: D2 antagonist, days, lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, slower evolution.
Serotonin toxicity: serotonergic agent, hours, clonus, hyperreflexia, shivering.
Malignant catatonia: prior catatonic features, may merge clinically with NMS.
Both: hyperthermia, AKI from rhabdomyolysis, autonomic instability.

options.rationale: Both NMS and severe serotonin syndrome cause hyperthermia above 40; temperature alone does not discriminate. Tone and reflexes separate the two more reliably (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

NMS classically follows D2 antagonist exposure or dose increase with bradykinesia, generalised lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes; serotonin toxicity produces hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limb) and shivering with a serotonergic agent (Source: eTG Psychotropic; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria).

Rhabdomyolysis and AKI occur in severe forms of both syndromes; CK is supportive but not discriminating. The CK rise reflects severity more than which syndrome is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Both syndromes feature altered conscious state and autonomic instability; necessary but non-specific. Would never be discriminating (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Posturing can occur in NMS, malignant catatonia, and extreme serotonin toxicity with substantial overlap with catatonia, so it does not separate NMS from serotonin syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis with the Hunter Criteria more sensitive and specific than the older Sternbach criteria. Triad of features is neuromuscular (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, rigidity), autonomic (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, mydriasis, diarrhoea), and altered mental state (agitation, confusion). Onset is within 24 hours of starting or increasing a serotonergic agent, or adding a second (the highest-risk combinations include MAOI plus SSRI, SSRI plus tramadol, fentanyl, ondansetron, linezolid, methylene blue, dextromethorphan, St John's wort, or recreational MDMA). Lower-limb spontaneous clonus is the most discriminating bedside finding. Differentiate from NMS (rigidity, hyporeflexia, slower onset, dopamine antagonist) and anticholinergic toxidrome (dry skin, urinary retention). Management is cessation of serotonergic agents, supportive care, benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, active cooling for hyperthermia, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally for non-responders. Severe cases need ICU.
key_points: Hunter Criteria require a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, ocular clonus, tremor with hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with T above 38 and ocular/inducible clonus.
Tramadol, fentanyl, MAOIs, linezolid, St John's wort all contribute to serotonin load.
Benzodiazepines are first-line pharmacotherapy.
Cyproheptadine 12 mg loading then 2 mg q2h for moderate toxicity not responding.
explanation.pearls: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, tremor plus hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 plus clonus. Cease serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines, supportive care (Hunter Criteria).

options.rationale: Mild to moderate serotonin toxicity is treated by withdrawing serotonergic agents, supportive care including IV fluids and cooling, and benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus; cyproheptadine is reserved for moderate-to-severe cases not responding to supportive care (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Serotonin toxicity; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria).

Bromocriptine is dopamine agonist used in some NMS protocols, not serotonin toxicity; this patient's hyperreflexia, clonus and serotonergic medication history indicate serotonin syndrome. Would be correct in NMS (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Benzatropine treats acute dystonia and parkinsonism from D2 blockade; no role in serotonin toxicity and anticholinergic effects can worsen hyperthermia. Would be correct in dystonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Dantrolene and neuromuscular blockade are reserved for life-threatening hyperthermia over 41.5 not responding to supportive measures; aggressive escalation here is premature. Would be correct only at life-threatening hyperthermia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Both venlafaxine and tramadol are serotonergic; switching to another SNRI while continuing tramadol perpetuates toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Two adequate trials at therapeutic dose with confirmed adherence define treatment-resistant schizophrenia, for which clozapine is the only superior agent. In Australia, clozapine is dispensed via registered programs (e.g. ClopineCentral, ClozaConnect) with mandatory haematological monitoring (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).
key_points: TRS criteria: failure of 2+ different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration with adherence.
Clozapine requires baseline FBC, ECG and registration on a monitoring service.
Polypharmacy and switching to another non-clozapine agent are not first-line.
Clozapine reduces all-cause mortality and suicide in schizophrenia.

options.rationale: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as failure of two adequate trials (>=6 weeks at therapeutic dose, adherence confirmed) of two different antipsychotics; clozapine is the only evidence-based pharmacotherapy and Australian use requires patient registration with a clozapine monitoring service (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016; AMH 2024).
Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not first-line for TRS and increases adverse effects without consistent efficacy benefit. (Source: RANZCP).
Deferring clozapine after two adequate trials prolongs symptom burden, functional impairment and suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP).
ECT is for catatonia, severe depression with psychosis, or augmentation in clozapine-resistant; not first-line for TRS. Would be correct after clozapine failure (Source: RANZCP).
LAIs address adherence not efficacy; adherence has been confirmed, so issue is treatment resistance. Would be correct only with non-adherence (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Clozapine carries a 0.7-1.2% risk of myocarditis, peaking between weeks 2 and 4 of titration, and a lower lifetime risk of cardiomyopathy. The Australian protocol mandates baseline ECG, troponin, CRP and echocardiogram before commencement, then weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks. Presentation is non-specific: chest pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, fever, tachycardia, often with rising troponin (more than 2x ULN), rising CRP and ECG changes (T-wave inversion, ST depression). Eosinophilia is supportive but not required. Any troponin rise above twice ULN with symptoms mandates immediate clozapine cessation, admission for cardiology review, urgent transthoracic echocardiogram, and notification of the clozapine registry (CPMS or ClopineCentral). Recovery is usual with cessation; rechallenge has been done but requires specialist input and tight monitoring. Mortality from missed myocarditis is significant. Hypersalivation, fever and chest pain in the first month are clozapine until proven otherwise.
key_points: Myocarditis window: weeks 2 to 4 (most), up to 8 weeks.
Red flags: fever, tachycardia, troponin rise, CRP >50, dyspnoea, eosinophilia.
Agranulocytosis cut-offs (general): Green N >=2.0, Amber 1.5 to 2.0, Red <1.5 (some programs use 1.0).
Other clozapine adverse effects: hypersalivation, constipation/ileus, seizures, weight gain, hyperglycaemia.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks at weeks 2-4 of titration with chest pain, dyspnoea, fever, fatigue and ECG changes; weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 weeks is the Australian protocol. Troponin rise plus symptoms = cease clozapine, urgent echo (TGA Clozapine PI; AMH).

options.rationale: Continuing clozapine in suspected myocarditis is contraindicated (progression to fulminant HF); aspirin alone is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP).

In the first 4 to 8 weeks of clozapine titration, fever with tachycardia and rising troponin and CRP suggests clozapine-induced myocarditis; immediate cessation, admission, troponin trend, ECG, and echocardiogram are mandated (Source: AMH 2024; eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine adverse effects; TGA Clozapine PI).
ANC 4.6 is normal; agranulocytosis is under 0.5; clozapine is interrupted (Amber) at 1.0-1.5 and ceased at under 1.0. (Source: ClopineCentral).
Dose reduction without cessation does not address myocarditis; beta blockade can mask haemodynamic deterioration. (Source: RANZCP).

Gallop, raised troponin and normal lung exam point to myocarditis not pneumonia; treating CAP without addressing cardiac picture is wrong. Would be correct only with documented CAP (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is under-recognised, can cause ileus, bowel ischaemia, perforation and death, and accounts for more clozapine-related deaths than agranulocytosis. The mechanism is anticholinergic and serotonergic suppression of GI motility, compounded by sedentary behaviour, sedation and constipating coprescribed medications. Risk is dose-related and persists lifelong. Australian guidance is daily bowel chart, prophylactic osmotic laxative (macrogol or lactulose) from initiation, and avoidance of constipating agents (loperamide, opioids, anticholinergics, tricyclics, antimuscarinic antihistamines). Any clozapine patient presenting with absent bowel motions for 3 days, abdominal pain, distension, vomiting or absent bowel sounds needs immediate admission, IV fluids, NG decompression, abdominal X-ray and surgical review. Treatment is aggressive osmotic and stimulant laxatives, prokinetics, and emergent surgery for perforation. CIGH is not an indication for stopping clozapine - the priority is treating the obstruction.
key_points: All clozapine patients need a documented bowel-monitoring plan and prophylactic laxatives.
Avoid loperamide, anticholinergics with high antimuscarinic load, and opioids where possible.
Overflow diarrhoea can mask severe constipation.
Mortality from ileus/perforation in clozapine cohorts exceeds that from agranulocytosis.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is fatal in around 1 in 1000 patients per year; constipation, abdominal pain or vomiting on clozapine = immediate admission for IV fluids, NG decompression, surgical review and aggressive osmotic laxatives. Avoid loperamide, opioids and anticholinergics (eTG; Cochrane).

options.rationale: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility can progress from chronic constipation to ileus, megacolon and bowel perforation; loperamide is contraindicated, and management requires admission, decompression, surgical review and stepwise laxative escalation (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Clozapine adverse effects; AMH 2024).
Outpatient management with bulk laxative in established ileus risks bowel perforation; bulking agents can worsen impaction. (Source: RANZCP; AMH).
Abrupt permanent cessation of clozapine in stable treatment-responsive patient risks severe relapse; standard is to manage GI complication. (Source: RANZCP).
Colonoscopy in suspected ileus or megacolon carries high perforation risk; AXR and CT abdomen preferred. Would never be correct as first investigation (Source: ANZ Gastro).
Metoclopramide is D2 antagonist that can cause EPSE and unlikely to reverse established large-bowel hypomotility; discharge unsafe. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal in heavy daily drinkers typically begins 6-12 hours after last drink, peaks at 48-72 hours, and resolves over 5-7 days. Severity is stratified with the CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol revised), with score over 15 indicating severe withdrawal. Australian standard management is symptom-triggered diazepam dosing (rather than fixed-schedule) titrated to CIWA-Ar - typically 10-20 mg PO every 1-2 hours - which has the same efficacy with lower total dose and shorter inpatient stay. Concurrent parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days) prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy, with magnesium replacement and aggressive electrolyte correction (potassium, phosphate). Prior seizures, prior delirium tremens, comorbid medical illness, or CIWA-Ar above 25 lower the threshold for ICU. Discharge planning includes naltrexone or acamprosate, counselling and ongoing engagement with addiction services.
key_points: Pabrinex (high-dose IV thiamine + B-complex) BD for 3 to 5 days for at-risk patients.
Oral thiamine alone is inadequate in alcoholic malnutrition.
Symptom-triggered diazepam outperforms fixed-dose regimens.
Correct hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia to reduce seizure risk.
explanation.pearls: Symptom-triggered diazepam (10-20 mg PO every 1-2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar) plus IV Pabrinex (2 pairs TDS for 3-5 days) is the Australian protocol for severe alcohol withdrawal; prior seizures or DTs lower the threshold for ICU admission (NSW Health; eTG Addiction).

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: CIWA-Ar 22 is severe withdrawal; observation alone risks progression to seizures or DTs; oral thiamine is insufficient prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing is the standard of care for severe alcohol withdrawal in Australian guidance; parenteral high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex) is required for Wernicke's prophylaxis in any heavy drinker with malnutrition risk, and electrolyte correction reduces seizure risk (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Anticonvulsants other than benzodiazepines are second-line and inferior for severe withdrawal; benzodiazepines are first-line. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Propofol infusion is for refractory DT in ICU; not appropriate on ward and not first-line. Would be correct in refractory DT in ICU (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Alcohol tapering is not used in AU inpatient practice; pharmacokinetic variability, hepatotoxicity and impaired titration make benzodiazepine-based withdrawal safer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Wernicke's encephalopathy is an acute, treatable, frequently missed thiamine-deficiency syndrome - autopsy series suggest it is recognised antemortem in under a third of cases. The full triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion is present in fewer than 20% of patients, so any malnourished, alcohol-dependent, hyperemetic or bariatric-surgery patient with unexplained neurological signs warrants empirical thiamine. Glucose without preceding or co-administered thiamine pushes pyruvate into glycolysis and precipitates or worsens encephalopathy. Australian practice is high-dose parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days, then taper) plus magnesium replacement (cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes). Untreated, 80% develop Korsakoff's amnestic syndrome and 20% die. Continue oral thiamine 100 mg daily at discharge with alcohol-use disorder management.
key_points: Empirical high-dose parenteral B-complex (Pabrinex) for any at-risk patient before glucose.
Magnesium is a thiamine cofactor and must be replaced.
Untreated Wernicke's progresses to irreversible Korsakoff syndrome.
Caine criteria: 2 of 4 - dietary deficiency, oculomotor abnormalities, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental state.
explanation.pearls: In suspected Wernicke's, give Pabrinex (IV thiamine 250 mg) BEFORE any glucose; glucose-first precipitates encephalopathy by accelerating thiamine consumption in glycolysis. Australian protocol is 2 pairs IV TDS for 3-5 days (eTG; NSW Health alcohol withdrawal).

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Suspected Wernicke's requires immediate parenteral high-dose B-complex (Pabrinex) before or with any glucose; magnesium is a cofactor and must be corrected for thiamine to be effective. Australian dosing is 2 pairs IV TDS for 3 to 5 days (Source: eTG Psychotropic: Wernicke's encephalopathy; NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Standard 100 mg IM thiamine is inadequate for established Wernicke's; high-dose parenteral B-complex BD-TDS for several days required. Would be correct only for prophylaxis not established WE (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Correcting hypoglycaemia must continue with concurrent thiamine; magnesium without thiamine does not reverse Wernicke's. Would be correct as part of full regimen, not as monotherapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Wernicke's is clinical diagnosis; delay for imaging risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia; treatment must be empirical. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
Oral absorption is unreliable in chronic alcohol use and inadequate for established encephalopathy; parenteral high-dose B-complex required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Naltrexone and acamprosate are the two first-line, PBS-listed pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder in Australian practice. Naltrexone (50 mg orally daily) is a mu-opioid antagonist that reduces the reinforcing effect of alcohol, decreasing cravings and heavy drinking - effective whether the goal is abstinence or reduction. Contraindications are current opioid use (including methadone or buprenorphine maintenance), opioid withdrawal (precipitates severe symptoms), acute hepatitis, and severe liver dysfunction (Child-Pugh C). Acamprosate (666 mg TDS) modulates NMDA and GABA-A receptors and supports continued abstinence after withdrawal; it requires the patient to be alcohol-free at initiation. The two can be combined for additive effect. Disulfiram (200-400 mg daily aversion therapy) is second-line and requires supervised dosing, cardiac and hepatic clearance, and committed motivation. Topiramate and gabapentin are off-label options. All pharmacotherapy is delivered alongside psychosocial intervention.
key_points: Confirm patient is opioid-free (urine drug screen) before naltrexone.
Acamprosate: maintain abstinence; dosed TDS by weight; renal excretion.
Disulfiram: requires supervised dosing and motivation; CVS/hepatic risks.
Pharmacotherapy is always combined with psychosocial support.
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone 50 mg daily is first-line PBS-listed AUD pharmacotherapy in Australia - reduces cravings and heavy drinking by acting at the mu-opioid receptor. Contraindicated in current opioid use, opioid withdrawal, severe liver dysfunction (RACGP/RANZCP AUD).

options.rationale: Naltrexone is first-line for AUD maintenance in patients not on opioids, reduces cravings and heavy-drinking days, and is appropriate where craving is the dominant symptom; it is contraindicated in current opioid use (Source: RACP/RANZCP Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of AUD; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).

Acamprosate is equally valid first-line (best for sustaining abstinence already achieved); naltrexone has stronger craving evidence. Would be correct when abstinence already achieved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Disulfiram requires high motivation, supervised dosing and acceptance of aversive reaction; second-line. Would be correct after first-line failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Benzodiazepines are for acute withdrawal only; ongoing use risks cross-dependence and is not maintenance therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Topiramate has some evidence but is off-label in AU and third-line; cognitive adverse effects notable in working woman. Would be correct only after first-line failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Disulfiram is a second- or third-line pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder used when first-line agents (naltrexone, acamprosate) have failed in motivated patients with committed abstinence goals. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so any alcohol ingestion produces acetaldehyde accumulation with flushing, headache, palpitations, nausea, vomiting and hypotension - the disulfiram-ethanol reaction (DER). The DER can be fatal in patients with cardiovascular disease, severe hepatic failure or significant electrolyte derangement; these are absolute contraindications, alongside pregnancy, psychosis (can precipitate decompensation), and inability to consent to supervised aversion therapy. Even hidden alcohol (mouthwash, cough syrup, vinegar, communion wine, fermented sauces) can trigger DER. Baseline ECG, LFTs, and informed consent documentation are mandatory. Standard dose 200-400 mg daily, ideally with supervised administration (partner or pharmacy daily pick-up). Hepatotoxicity in 1 in 30000 requires monthly LFTs initially.
key_points: Avoid in IHD, severe HTN, recent MI/stroke, severe liver failure, psychosis.
Counsel about all ethanol sources (cough mixtures, mouthwash, aftershave, sauces).
LFTs at baseline, 2 and 6 weeks, then 3 to 6 monthly.
Reaction onset is 10 to 30 minutes after ethanol, can last several hours.
explanation.pearls: Disulfiram contraindications: significant cardiovascular disease (the disulfiram-ethanol reaction can cause hypotension, MI, arrhythmia, death), severe hepatic failure, pregnancy, psychosis, and inability to consent to supervised aversion therapy (eTG Addiction; AMH).

options.rationale: Significant cardiovascular disease (including ischaemic heart disease, severe hypertension, recent MI or stroke) is a contraindication to disulfiram because the disulfiram-ethanol reaction can precipitate severe hypertension, arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse (Source: eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).
Severe hepatic impairment is contraindication; compensated Child-Pugh A is caution requiring LFT monitoring, not absolute bar. Would be correct only with severe impairment (Source: AMH).
Metoprolol has no specific contraindication with disulfiram. (Source: AMH).
Age alone is not contraindication; risk-benefit individualised. (Source: AMH).
No clinically significant interaction precluding co-prescription of atorvastatin with disulfiram. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine-naloxone induction in established moderate withdrawal (COWS >=12) is preferred for community OST, especially for patients with limited capacity for daily supervised dispensing. Methadone is started low and titrated slowly because of accumulation and overdose risk (Source: NGMA; eTG Addiction).
key_points: Methadone day 1: 20 to 30 mg, max 40 mg; steady state at 5 days.
Buprenorphine: lower overdose risk, ceiling on respiratory depression, faster stabilisation.
Precipitated withdrawal: occurs if buprenorphine given too early.
ECG before methadone if dose >100 mg or QT-prolonging meds; review at 1 month.

sources.label: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Buprenorphine is preferred over methadone for community induction because of lower overdose risk, capacity for unsupervised takeaway doses earlier, and shorter induction; it must only be given once moderate withdrawal is established (COWS >=12) to avoid precipitated withdrawal (Source: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Methadone induction starts low (20-30 mg, no more than 40 mg day 1) due to long half-life and accumulation risk; 60 mg day 1 has caused fatal overdoses. (Source: NSW Health Methadone Guideline).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Oral naltrexone has very high relapse rates in opioid dependence and is not first-line maintenance; cannot start until 7-10 days opioid-free. Would be correct in highly motivated abstinence-focused patients (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Naloxone reverses overdose, not for confirming dependence; deliberate precipitation of withdrawal is unethical. (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Day-1 buprenorphine should start at 2-8 mg with cautious top-up; 16 mg risks oversedation. Would be correct only at later titration (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

explanation.summary: Methadone prolongs QTc and accumulates when CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, macrolides, HIV PIs) are introduced; combined with benzodiazepines, overdose risk rises. Australian OST guidance recommends ECG before methadone if dose >100 mg or QT-prolonging meds, repeat at 1 month and after dose or interacting-drug changes (Source: NGMA).
key_points: QT-prolonging interactions: azoles, macrolides, ondansetron, SSRIs, antipsychotics, HIV PIs.
QTc >500 ms is a strong indication to switch from methadone to buprenorphine.
Concurrent benzodiazepines markedly increase overdose mortality.
Naloxone supply and overdose education are part of routine OST care.

sources.label: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Fluconazole inhibits methadone metabolism (CYP3A4/CYP2B6) and prolongs QT; diphenhydramine adds anticholinergic load and QT effect; the priority is removing the offending agents, addressing benzodiazepine use, and re-evaluating with repeat ECG, with a switch to buprenorphine if QT remains prolonged (Source: NGMA; eTG Addiction; AMH 2024).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: QTc 510 ms carries significant torsades risk and demands prompt action; passive review is unsafe. (Source: AMH).
Increasing methadone worsens QT prolongation and overdose risk, particularly with co-ingested benzodiazepines. (Source: AMH).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Abrupt methadone cessation precipitates withdrawal and relapse; naltrexone cannot start until 7-10 days opioid-free. (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: National Guidelines for Medication-Assisted Treatment of Opioid Dependence (NGMA)

options.rationale: Beta-blockers reduce risk in congenital LQTS but not standard response to drug-induced QT prolongation; correct approach is to identify and remove QT-prolonging drugs. Would be correct only in congenital LQTS (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance (ABD) from methamphetamine or other stimulants presents with severe agitation, paranoid psychosis, hypertensive crisis, hyperthermia, and risk of self-harm or harm to others. The NSW Health ABD Guideline and eTG Toxicology recommend IM droperidol 10 mg as first-line in a monitored ED resuscitation bay - droperidol has rapid onset, sedates without dropping BP, and is well-tolerated. Cautious IM midazolam 2.5-5 mg can be added for ongoing agitation, titrated to effect to avoid respiratory depression. Restrain only if needed for safety, with continuous monitoring of vital signs, SpO2, ECG, and core temperature. Anticipate stimulant complications: hyperthermia above 39 requires active cooling, rhabdomyolysis warrants CK and fluid resuscitation, hypertensive emergency may need short-acting vasodilator, and acute coronary syndromes occur even in young patients. Avoid haloperidol IV (QT prolongation in cocaine and methamphetamine). Once stabilised, brief psychiatric assessment, social supports, and addiction medicine referral.
key_points: Treat the patient, monitor airway/breathing/circulation continuously after sedation.
Cool, hydrate, assess for rhabdomyolysis (CK), check ECG and electrolytes.
Avoid pure beta-blockade for stimulant hypertension (unopposed alpha effect); use benzodiazepines first.
Methamphetamine-induced psychosis typically resolves within 1 week with abstinence; persistent symptoms warrant psychiatric review.
explanation.pearls: Severe acute behavioural disturbance from methamphetamine: IM droperidol 10 mg in a monitored area, with cautious IM midazolam 2.5-5 mg titrated for agitation. Anticipate stimulant hyperthermia (above 39 = active cooling), rhabdomyolysis, dysrhythmia (NSW Health ABD).

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.rationale: Australian ED guidance for severe stimulant-related acute behavioural disturbance recommends parenteral droperidol with cautious adjunctive midazolam in a monitored setting, reflecting NSW Health protocols; this rapidly controls agitation while minimising oversedation (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance; eTG Toxicology).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.rationale: Oral medication is unsafe and impractical for severe ABD with imminent harm; parenteral in monitored area required. Would be correct only for mild agitation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for refractory cases when droperidol and benzodiazepine have failed (laryngospasm, hypertension, airway risks). Would be correct only as refractory (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.rationale: IV haloperidol carries higher QT/torsades risk than IM droperidol and is not preferred in AU ABD protocols. Would be correct only if droperidol unavailable (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint without sedation risks asphyxia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and sudden death in stimulant intoxication. (Source: ANZICS).
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance in ED

explanation.summary: Acute mania with refusal of treatment and risk to self meets criteria for involuntary admission under state MHAs. The least-restrictive principle still applies, but inpatient assessment is required before any community treatment order can be considered (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007).
key_points: Schedules/forms vary by state but principles are similar: presence of mental illness, risk of serious harm, no less restrictive option.
Common-law restraint is for immediate, brief safety - not ongoing treatment.
Community treatment orders follow tribunal processes after inpatient assessment.
Capacity is decision-specific and is impaired by acute mania with grandiose delusions.

options.rationale: She meets criteria as a mentally ill person (presence of mental illness, behaviour requires treatment to protect her from serious harm including risk to her health/safety such as exhaustion, financial harm) and is refusing voluntary admission; the MHA assessment schedule and admission to a declared facility for AMO review is the appropriate pathway (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007; RANZCP).
Severe sleep deprivation, escalating manic behaviour and refusal of treatment make outpatient unsafe in next 24 h. (Source: NSW MHA).

Common-law restraint is for emergency intervention to prevent immediate harm, not primary framework for ongoing detention and treatment. Would be correct only briefly during emergency (Source: NSW MHA).
CTOs are made by MHRT following inpatient assessment with specific procedural steps; cannot be made directly from ED. (Source: NSW MHA).
She lacks capacity to refuse treatment due to grandiose delusions and lack of insight; MHA exists to address this. (Source: NSW MHA).

explanation.summary: TD presents months to years after antipsychotic use as involuntary orofacial movements. First-line management is to switch to a lower-TD-risk antipsychotic (clozapine has the strongest evidence). VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are emerging but not yet PBS-listed in Australia for routine TD treatment (Source: eTG Psychotropic).
key_points: AIMS assessed 6-monthly in patients on long-term antipsychotics.
Anticholinergics can worsen TD; cease them if possible.
Increasing the offending agent only masks the disorder.
Risk factors: older age, female, first-generation antipsychotics, long duration, prior EPSE.

options.rationale: Anticholinergics do not improve and may worsen TD; benzatropine helps acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, not TD. Would be correct in acute dystonia or parkinsonism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Long-term first-generation antipsychotic exposure is the major risk factor for TD; switching to a second-generation antipsychotic with lower TD risk (clozapine has the strongest evidence) is the recommended strategy (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG 2016).
Polypharmacy increases adverse-effect burden including TD; combining second D2 antagonist worsens pathology. (Source: RANZCP).
Increasing offending antipsychotic transiently masks TD but worsens long-term course; contraindicated as management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Abrupt cessation can cause withdrawal dyskinesia and risks psychotic relapse; switching to lower-risk agent preferred. Would never be correct as planned strategy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a unique pharmacological profile of rapidly lost tolerance: stopping for as little as 48 hours requires re-titration from the starting dose (12.5 mg) following the standard induction schedule (typically 5-14 days back to therapeutic dose). Restarting at the previous stable dose risks profound hypotension, sedation, anticholinergic delirium, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmia, with reported deaths from medication errors at this transition. Common scenarios prompting re-titration include travel, hospital admission (where clozapine is often omitted due to unfamiliarity), incarceration, refusal during relapse, and supply disruption. The Australian clozapine registry (CPMS or ClopineCentral) coordinates re-initiation: confirm registry status, baseline FBC, ECG, troponin and CRP repeated, then titrate per protocol. During re-titration, weekly FBC, troponin and CRP are required for 4 weeks because myocarditis risk re-emerges with the re-titration window. Patient education on the importance of unbroken supply is part of every clozapine review.
key_points: Restart from 12.5 mg if 2+ days missed; up-titrate cautiously per protocol.
Add prophylactic anticonvulsant in high-risk patients with prior clozapine-related seizures.
Smoking induces CYP1A2; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels.
Communicate any change in smoking, dose or interacting drugs to the clozapine service.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine tolerance is lost rapidly: missed doses for 48 hours or more mandate full re-titration from 12.5 mg, regardless of previous stable dose. Skipping retitration risks hypotension, sedation, seizures and cardiac arrhythmia (TGA Clozapine PI).

options.rationale: After 48+ h without clozapine, tolerance is lost; resuming previous full dose markedly increases orthostatic hypotension, seizure and sedation risk. (Source: AMH).

Australian and manufacturer guidance is that after 2 or more days of missed clozapine doses, the drug must be re-titrated from the starting dose because tolerance to orthostatic hypotension, sedation and seizure risk is rapidly lost; this is particularly important given his prior seizure history (Source: Clozapine product information TGA; eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP).
Halving does not safely re-establish tolerance and still carries significant risk; protocol requires retitration from 12.5 mg. (Source: AMH).
Switching from clozapine should be planned (relapse risk high); unplanned switch is unsafe and not indicated for missed-dose period. (Source: RANZCP).

Anticonvulsant prophylaxis is considered for higher-risk patients during retitration but does not replace requirement to retitrate from start. Would be correct as adjunct, not replacement (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens has a mortality of 5 to 15% untreated. Australian management is escalation to high-acuity care, parenteral benzodiazepines (lorazepam preferred in significant hepatic impairment because of pharmacokinetics), and aggressive electrolyte correction with high-dose B-complex (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines).
key_points: DT onset 48 to 96 hours after last drink; mortality without treatment up to 15%.
Lorazepam is preferred over diazepam in significant hepatic dysfunction.
Always replace thiamine before/with glucose and correct magnesium.
Antipsychotics only as adjunct for severe hallucinations after benzodiazepine optimisation.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Delirium tremens with refractory agitation and seizures is a medical emergency requiring high-acuity care; in significant hepatic impairment, lorazepam (less hepatic metabolism, no active metabolites) is preferred over diazepam, with aggressive electrolyte correction (Source: NSW Health Withdrawal Guidelines; eTG Addiction; eTG Critical Care).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Oral diazepam in confused, seizing, vomiting patient is unreliable; severe DT requires parenteral therapy and high-acuity monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and don't treat underlying GABA deficit; benzodiazepines are first-line in DT with low-dose antipsychotic only as adjunct. Would be correct only as adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for alcohol-withdrawal seizures (GABA-mediated); benzodiazepines are both treatment and prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Naloxone has no role in alcohol withdrawal; it is opioid antagonist for opioid overdose. Would never be correct in alcohol withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 moved decisively away from the 'medically unexplained symptoms' framing of DSM-IV somatoform disorders, recognising that genuine medical conditions and psychiatric distress frequently coexist. Somatic symptom disorder is now defined by the disproportionate cognitive, affective and behavioural response to somatic symptoms: persistent thoughts about seriousness, anxiety, and excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms or health concerns. Symptoms can be medically explained, unexplained, or partially explained - the diagnosis turns on the response, not the aetiology. SSD is a positive diagnosis based on observable clinical features and is made alongside any organic diagnosis rather than as a diagnosis of exclusion. Management is multidisciplinary: a single trusted primary clinician coordinates care, scheduled regular follow-up replaces symptom-driven attendance, investigations are minimised, comorbid mood and anxiety are treated, and CBT for SSD addresses the cognitive-behavioural reaction. Reassurance alone does not work; structured engagement does.
key_points: SSD = >=1 distressing somatic symptom + disproportionate thoughts/anxiety/behaviours + >6 months
Illness anxiety disorder centres on feared disease with little or no somatic symptom
FND requires positive neurological incompatibility signs
Factitious disorder requires deceptive intent without external incentive
explanation.pearls: DSM-5 somatic symptom disorder requires one or more somatic symptoms causing distress or disruption, with disproportionate thoughts, anxiety or time/energy devoted to the symptoms; symptoms can be medically explained or unexplained - the criterion is the disproportionate response, not the absence of explanation (DSM-5; RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Illness anxiety disorder requires preoccupation with HAVING or acquiring a serious illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms; her dominant feature is the symptoms themselves. Would be correct only with minimal somatic symptoms (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: DSM-5 SSD requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms PLUS disproportionate or persistent thoughts, anxiety, or behaviours about them, for more than 6 months. Her persistent pain, excessive health-related time use, functional decline, and disproportionate concern across 18 months meet criteria; persistent course is specified at >6 months of severe symptoms (DSM-5; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: GAD requires excessive worry across multiple domains for 6+ months with 3+ of restlessness/fatigue/concentration/irritability/muscle tension/sleep; her concern centres on her somatic symptoms instead. Would be correct in multi-domain worry pattern (Source: DSM-5).

FND requires altered voluntary motor/sensory function with positive incompatibility signs (Hoover's, tremor entrainment); abdominal pain and fatigue do not fit. Would be correct with positive incompatibility signs (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Factitious requires intentional falsification or induction of signs/symptoms with deceptive intent without obvious external reward; absent here. Would be correct with deception (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis. Hoover's sign (involuntary recovery of hip extension during contralateral hip flexion) is the bedside test that rules in functional leg weakness. Treatment hinges on a clear non-blaming explanation plus FND-specific physiotherapy (FND Society 2021).
key_points: FND positive signs: Hoover's, hip abductor sign, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness with normal reflexes
Communicate diagnosis as real, common, and treatable; avoid 'nothing wrong'
FND-specific physiotherapy has the strongest evidence base
Psychological therapy is adjunctive, not primary
explanation.pearls: If MRI is normal AND a positive sign is present, you have rule-in evidence - say so explicitly to the patient (FND Society).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Stroke is unlikely with normal MRI, symmetric reflexes, flexor plantar, positive Hoover's indicating functional weakness; antiplatelets in this setting harms without benefit. Would be correct in confirmed stroke (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
MS is excluded by normal MRI and positive functional sign; steroids would entrench illness behaviour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Telling FND patients 'nothing is wrong' worsens distress, increases relapse and is associated with poorer outcomes; FND is a positive diagnosis to be communicated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).

FND is a positive diagnosis based on incompatibility signs (Hoover's, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness with normal MRI and reflexes). The first therapeutic step is a clear, non-stigmatising explanation that the diagnosis is made BY the positive sign, framed as a brain functioning problem that is treatable, followed by referral to FND-trained physiotherapy which is the strongest evidence-based intervention (RANZCP; FND Society Consensus; NICE NG217 stroke excluded).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for FND and inpatient psychiatric admission is rarely indicated; physiotherapy is the evidence-based primary treatment. (Source: BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is dominated by fear of having or acquiring a serious illness with minimal somatic symptoms; SSD is dominated by distressing somatic symptoms themselves. The useful question is whether the patient is distressed by the symptom or by what the symptom means (DSM-5).
key_points: IAD: feared disease + minimal somatic symptoms + >6 months + health-related behaviours
Care-seeking type repeatedly investigates; care-avoidant type avoids medical contact
Reassurance provides only short-term relief, a hallmark feature
Differentiate from delusional disorder by reality testing
explanation.pearls: If reassurance helps for 24 hours then doubt returns, think illness anxiety, not delusion (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: SSD requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms as focus; his somatic symptoms are minor and dominant feature is fear of having pancreatic cancer. Would be correct with predominant somatic symptoms (Source: DSM-5).
GAD requires worry across multiple domains for 6+ months; his worry is narrowly focused on single feared disease (illness anxiety pattern). Would be correct in multi-domain worry (Source: DSM-5).

DSM-5 illness anxiety disorder: preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness; somatic symptoms are absent or mild; high health-related anxiety; excessive health-related behaviours OR maladaptive avoidance; duration >=6 months; not better explained by another disorder. Repeated investigations, reassurance-seeking, and forum use mark the care-seeking type (DSM-5; RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: OCD requires obsessions and/or compulsions consuming over 1 hour daily; his behaviours are health-focused reassurance-seeking, not classical OCD. Would be correct with classical OCD obsessions (Source: DSM-5).

Delusional disorder somatic type requires fixed false beliefs of bodily disease with delusional intensity; he accepts reassurance partially. Would be correct with delusional intensity (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

explanation.summary: Factitious disorder vs malingering hinges on motivation: factitious is intentional symptom production motivated by the sick role with NO external incentive; malingering is intentional symptom production for external incentive (benefits, avoidance, drugs). Suppressed C-peptide with elevated insulin is a textbook signature of surreptitious insulin use (DSM-5; AMH).
key_points: Factitious disorder: intentional + deceptive + no external incentive (sick-role motive)
Malingering: intentional + deceptive + external incentive
Suppressed C-peptide + high insulin + negative sulfonylurea = exogenous insulin
Approach: avoid confrontation, address underlying psychological need, consult-liaison referral
explanation.pearls: Document objective evidence of induction (lab pattern, hidden items) before formulating - confrontation typically escalates the behaviour (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Malingering requires EXTERNAL incentive (financial, legal, evasion of duty, drug-seeking); he has no claim, litigation, forensic process. Would be correct with external incentive (Source: DSM-5).
source_refs: DSM-5-TR Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Three DSM-5 criteria are met: (i) falsification of physical signs (covertly self-administered insulin, evidenced by suppressed C-peptide with elevated insulin and observed sharps disposal); (ii) presentation as ill/injured/impaired; (iii) absence of obvious external incentive. The internal psychological gain (sick-role identity, relational connection with medical teams) separates this from malingering and is consistent with his nursing-background insider-knowledge profile.
SSD involves genuine somatic symptoms with disproportionate thoughts/feelings/behaviours; deliberate falsification takes case out of SSD. Would be correct with genuine symptoms (Source: DSM-5).

Conversion requires neurological symptoms (weakness, tremor, sensory loss) without organic cause; biochemical hypoglycaemia is not neurological. Would be correct with neurological symptoms (Source: DSM-5).

Delusional disorder requires fixed false belief; he is engaged in covert behaviour (sharps disposal) implying awareness of deception, inconsistent with delusional intensity. Would be correct with delusional intensity (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Before labelling a depressive presentation as primary, screen for medical mimics with TSH at minimum. Bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation, goitre, and an autoimmune family history make hypothyroidism a leading mimic and a treatable cause of mood and cognitive symptoms (RANZCP; eTG).
key_points: Baseline screen for mood presentations: TSH, FBC, UEC, LFTs, B12/folate, glucose, urine drug screen if indicated
Hypothyroid mimic features: bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation, dry skin, goitre, cold intolerance
TPO antibodies confirm Hashimoto
Empirical levothyroxine without bloods risks thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Treatment-resistant depression with no baseline TSH is a diagnostic red flag, not a pharmacological problem (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Switching antidepressants without first excluding medical mimic risks treating thyroid disease as treatment-resistant depression; AMH and RANZCP mandate exclusion of medical cause. Would never be correct without thyroid workup (Source: RANZCP).

Cushing screening is for features suggestive of cortisol excess (central adiposity, striae, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia); absent here. Would be correct with Cushing features (Source: APEG).
MRI not first-line with clear thyroid-pointing physical findings and no focal neurology; low pre-test probability. Would be correct with focal neuro findings (Source: RANZCR).

Clinical features (bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation, goitre, cold intolerance, weight gain, family history of autoimmune thyroid disease) point to primary hypothyroidism, most likely Hashimoto. TSH plus free T4 is the screening pair; TPO antibodies confirm autoimmune aetiology and guide monitoring of subclinical disease. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines require excluding thyroid disease before labelling depression as primary (RANZCP; eTG).
AMH requires confirmed biochemical hypothyroidism before levothyroxine to avoid iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the highest-yield psychiatric mimic to recognise in young women presenting with sub-acute psychosis plus movement disorder, autonomic instability, seizures, and lymphocytic CSF. Early antibody testing and immunotherapy improve outcomes; first-pass treatment as primary psychosis worsens prognosis (Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
key_points: Pentad: psychiatric symptoms, movement disorder, seizures, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly raised protein
Test BOTH serum and CSF NMDAR antibodies (CSF is more sensitive)
Look for ovarian teratoma once antibody confirmed
Antipsychotics can paradoxically worsen presentation (NMS-like)
explanation.pearls: If a young woman with new psychosis has orofacial dyskinesias before any antipsychotic exposure, think NMDAR encephalitis (Lancet Neurology consensus).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Multi-step: the prodromal flu-like illness, subacute psychiatric onset, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis form the classical anti-NMDAR encephalitis syndrome (Dalmau triad-plus).
