Definitive diagnosis requires BOTH serum and CSF antibodies (CSF more sensitive); MRI brain frequently normal but indicated for differential. While awaiting antibody result and HSV PCR, empirical aciclovir is standard because HSV encephalitis is treatable and the cost of delay is high. This combines confirmatory and empirical limbs concurrently.
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Immunology autoimmune encephalitis consensus

options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic in suspected autoimmune encephalitis worsens autonomic instability and dyskinesias, may precipitate NMS-overlap, and delays diagnosis. (Source: Titulaer 2013).
HSV cover is appropriate but failing to send autoimmune encephalitis antibodies delays diagnosis driving first-line immunotherapy. Would never be correct alone (Source: Titulaer 2013).
NMS requires antipsychotic exposure; she has had none. CK is only mildly raised. EEG useful adjunct but not the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Ovarian teratoma screening is ONCE anti-NMDAR antibodies confirm syndrome (then pelvic US/MRI first-line, not PET CT). Would be correct after antibody confirmation (Source: Titulaer 2013).

explanation.summary: Delirium superimposed on dementia complicates around 40% of medical admissions in older patients and is associated with significant morbidity, mortality and accelerated cognitive decline. The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care Delirium Clinical Care Standard prioritises identification, prevention and reversible-precipitant management over pharmacological sedation. Diagnose with CAM or 4AT: acute change from baseline, fluctuating course, inattention, plus either disorganised thinking or altered level of consciousness. Drivers are encapsulated in the PINCH-ME mnemonic - Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medications, Environment. First-line management is deprescribing iatrogenic precipitants (opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, metoclopramide), treating reversible drivers (UTI, pneumonia, retention, constipation, dehydration, electrolytes), and orientation, lighting, hearing/visual aids, family presence, mobilisation, and sleep hygiene. Pharmacological sedation (low-dose haloperidol, risperidone) is reserved for severe agitation with risk of harm; avoid in Parkinson's and Lewy body dementia.
key_points: DSM-5 delirium: acute change, fluctuation, inattention, additional cognitive disturbance, not better explained by dementia alone
First step: address deliriogenic medications, constipation, pain, hypoxia, hydration, sleep
Antipsychotics only for severe agitation with safety risk, lowest effective dose, short duration
Avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults
explanation.pearls: In hospital delirium, deprescribe the precipitant rather than adding sedation: high-yield culprits are opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics (oxybutynin, antihistamines, tricyclics) and metoclopramide; treat reversible drivers (pain, constipation, retention, infection, dehydration) (eTG; Australian Delirium Standard).

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care - Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.rationale: Adding antipsychotics without first deprescribing the precipitating drugs is wrong order; lorazepam and oxycodone are independent deliriogens. Would never be correct as initial step (Source: ACSQHC).
Cholinesterase inhibitors are not delirium treatment; discharge of actively delirious patient with unsafe medications breaches standard. (Source: ACSQHC).
Delirium is medical emergency managed on medical/geriatric ward; psychiatric ward transfer inappropriate and worsens outcome. (Source: ACSQHC).

ACSQHC standard sequence: identify and remove precipitants first. Lorazepam, oxycodone, metoclopramide and constipation are all reversible contributors. Asymptomatic bacteriuria/pyuria in older adults should NOT be treated (eTG), and over-treatment of dipstick findings is a major contributor to inappropriate antibiotic use and further delirium. Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation when non-pharmacological measures fail.
Asymptomatic pyuria in 84-year-old should not be treated; ciprofloxacin adds delirium risk (CNS effects). (Source: ACSQHC; Choosing Wisely).

explanation.summary: RANZCP defines TRD as failure of two adequate antidepressant trials. Lithium augmentation (target 0.4-0.8 mmol/L) and atypical antipsychotic augmentation (quetiapine or aripiprazole) are first-line; mirtazapine combination is reasonable; ECT is reserved for severe or rapid-response indications (RANZCP CPG 2020).
key_points: TRD = inadequate response to 2 adequate trials at therapeutic dose and duration
Lithium augmentation target 0.4-0.8 mmol/L (lower than mood stabilisation)
Baseline U+E, TSH, calcium, ECG before lithium; recheck level after 5-7 days
ECT indicated for catatonia, food refusal, high suicide risk, psychotic depression
Avoid benzodiazepines as augmentation
explanation.pearls: Lithium augmentation works within 2-4 weeks - re-evaluate at week 4, not week 12 (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Lithium augmentation has the strongest evidence base (multiple RCTs, NNT ~5) for SSRI/SNRI-resistant unipolar MDD and is the standard first augmentation in RANZCP TRD pathway. Target trough for augmentation is lower than mania prophylaxis (0.4-0.8 vs 0.6-1.0). The patient meets TRD criteria (two adequate trials) and has no contraindication (normal eGFR, normal TSH).
Switching to third antidepressant monotherapy has lower evidence than lithium or atypical-antipsychotic augmentation in TRD. (Source: RANZCP CPG).
Bupropion combination has weaker evidence than lithium/aripiprazole/quetiapine augmentation and is not PBS-listed for depression in Australia. (Source: TGA).
Benzodiazepines are not disease-modifying augmentation in TRD and add dependence risk; not supported. (Source: RANZCP).

ECT is for life-threatening (catatonia, food refusal, immediate suicide risk, severe psychotic depression) or after failure of multiple augmentations. Would be correct after augmentation failure (Source: RANZCP).

explanation.summary: Switching from fluoxetine to a non-selective irreversible MAOI requires a 5-week washout because norfluoxetine has a half-life of 7-15 days. Other SSRI/SNRI to MAOI switches require 2 weeks; MAOI to another antidepressant requires 2 weeks for enzyme regeneration (AMH; eTG).
key_points: Fluoxetine to MAOI: 5-week washout (norfluoxetine half-life)
Other SSRI/SNRI to MAOI: 2-week washout
MAOI to another antidepressant: 2-week washout (enzyme regeneration)
Cross-taper and direct switch SSRI to MAOI are contraindicated
Watch for serotonergic drug interactions: tramadol, triptans, linezolid, St John's Wort, pethidine
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine's washout rules dominate any switching plan involving an MAOI (AMH).

options.rationale: Direct switch from any serotonergic agent to MAOI risks fatal serotonin syndrome. Contraindicated. (Source: AMH).
Overlapping serotonergic agents with irreversible MAOI is contraindicated; cross-tapers are for SSRI-to-SSRI/SNRI switches. (Source: AMH).

Fluoxetine's active metabolite norfluoxetine has a half-life of 7-15 days; ~5 elimination half-lives = ~35-75 days. The AMH and eTG specify a 5-week minimum washout from fluoxetine to MAOI. Other SSRIs require ~2 weeks (5 half-lives of citalopram/sertraline).
5 days is grossly inadequate for fluoxetine because of norfluoxetine accumulation; 5-week wait required. (Source: AMH).
Co-administration of any SSRI with MAOI is contraindicated due to serotonin syndrome risk; no low-dose is safe. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Three features separate serotonin syndrome, NMS, and anticholinergic toxidrome: TIMING (SS hours; NMS days; anticholinergic hours), TONE (SS hyperreflexia + clonus; NMS lead-pipe rigidity + hyporeflexia; anticholinergic flaccid), and SKIN (SS and NMS sweaty; anticholinergic dry). Clonus, especially lower-limb and ocular, is the SS fingerprint (Hunter criteria; eTG).
key_points: SS: hours to onset, hyperreflexia, clonus (esp. lower limb + ocular), moist skin
NMS: days to onset, lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, moist skin, very high CK
Anticholinergic: hours to onset, dry skin/mucosae, mydriasis, urinary retention, NO clonus
Hunter criteria for SS require serotonergic exposure + one specific neuromuscular pattern
Treatment: stop all serotonergic drugs, cooling, IV benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine in severe cases
explanation.pearls: Linezolid is a hidden MAOI - combining with any serotonergic agent is high-risk (AMH).

options.rationale: Anticholinergic has DRY skin/mucosae, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds; patient's skin is MOIST with hyperreflexia. Would be correct with anticholinergic features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
NMS has lead-pipe rigidity, HYPOreflexia, autonomic instability, hyperthermia AND recent antipsychotic; patient has none of those. Would be correct in NMS phenotype (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Hunter criteria require serotonergic agent PLUS one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; tremor + hyperreflexia; hypertonia + temperature >38 + ocular/inducible clonus. He meets multiple. Triple-serotonergic exposure: SSRI + tramadol (weak SNRI/opioid with serotonergic activity) + linezolid (non-selective MAOI). Distinct from NMS by hyperreflexia/clonus pattern and absence of antipsychotic exposure.

Sympathomimetic shares tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, diaphoresis but lacks prominent neuromuscular features (hyperreflexia, clonus). Would be correct only with documented stimulant use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Malignant hyperthermia requires exposure to volatile anaesthetic or depolarising NMB; no exposure here. Would be correct only with anaesthetic exposure (Source: ANZCA).

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L maintenance, toxicity often >1.5 mmol/L). NSAID, ACE inhibitor/ARB, thiazide diuretic and dehydration are the four high-yield precipitants. Australian toxicology thresholds support dialysis at level >4.0 mmol/L, or 2.5-4.0 with significant neurotoxicity or impaired renal clearance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AMH).
key_points: Therapeutic range 0.6-0.8 (maintenance); toxicity threshold >1.5 mmol/L
Precipitants: NSAID, ACE-I/ARB, thiazide, dehydration, sodium depletion, AKI
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium
Volume repletion with isotonic saline is first-line; avoid loop diuretics
Haemodialysis indicated >4.0 mmol/L, or 2.5-4.0 with neurotoxicity or renal failure
explanation.pearls: Three drug interactions to remember: NSAID + ACE-I + thiazide all increase lithium level by 25-40% (AMH).

options.rationale: Lithium 2.1 with neurological features is moderate-to-severe toxicity; continuing risks progression to seizures, coma, irreversible nephrotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Acute toxicity with neuro features and AKI requires immediate cessation and inpatient management; week delay risks fatal progression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium (an ion); ineffective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
Loop diuretics WORSEN lithium toxicity (reduce volume, increase proximal tubular reabsorption); volume repletion with isotonic saline is correct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).

Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and AMH require: cease lithium immediately, withdraw precipitants (NSAID, ACE inhibitor, dehydration are the classic three), give IV crystalloid to restore intravascular volume, and consider haemodialysis. Australian thresholds for dialysis: level >4.0 mmol/L irrespective of symptoms, OR level 2.5-4.0 with significant neurotoxicity (confusion, seizures, decreased consciousness) or renal impairment limiting clearance. He sits at 2.1 with AKI - imminent dialysis consult is appropriate, particularly with rising level given renal impairment (eTG Toxicology; AMH).

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in any woman of childbearing potential without a Pregnancy Prevention Program due to major malformation (~10%) and neurodevelopmental impairment (~30-40%) risks. Quetiapine is the first-line alternative in pre-conception planning; lithium can be continued with informed consent; carbamazepine carries neural tube risk; lamotrigine does not prevent mania (RANZCP; TGA).
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: ~10% major malformations, ~30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment
Australian TGA restriction: avoid in women of childbearing potential without PPP
Quetiapine first-line atypical in bipolar pregnancy planning
Lamotrigine prevents bipolar DEPRESSION not MANIA
Lithium continuation requires fetal cardiac scan at 18-20 weeks
explanation.pearls: If a question mentions both bipolar AND a woman of reproductive age, valproate is almost always the wrong answer (TGA; RANZCP).

options.rationale: Adding valproate in woman of reproductive potential who has stopped contraception is contraindicated under TGA Valproate PPP. (Source: TGA).

Her predominant pattern is mania despite therapeutic lithium; the evidence base supports atypical antipsychotic adjunct (quetiapine, olanzapine) for breakthrough mania. Quetiapine has a more reassuring preconception profile than valproate, no Pregnancy Prevention Program, and acceptable monitoring requirements. Lithium is retained because her trough is therapeutic and switching would risk further mania during the planning window.
Carbamazepine is teratogenic (NTDs), induces hepatic enzymes (OCP interactions) and has weaker mania prophylaxis evidence. (Source: AMH).
Lithium absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is ~1-2 per 1000 (modest); stopping without replacement risks relapse. (Source: COPE).
Lamotrigine has efficacy for bipolar DEPRESSION prophylaxis but is INFERIOR to lithium for mania prophylaxis. Would be correct only in depression-predominant bipolar (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by fast sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension, and ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate is the targeted therapy: indications are QRS >100 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia, or seizures. Bolus 1-2 mmol/kg, repeat to narrow QRS and target pH 7.50-7.55 (Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology).
key_points: Bicarbonate indications: QRS >100 ms, terminal R in aVR >3 mm, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia, seizures
Contraindicated antiarrhythmics: class Ia, Ic, and III (amiodarone, procainamide, flecainide)
Flumazenil contraindicated in mixed TCA ingestions
Physostigmine contraindicated in TCA overdose
Activated charcoal within 1-2 hours only if alert with protected airway
explanation.pearls: Terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm is the most specific bedside marker of TCA cardiotoxicity (eTG).

options.rationale: TCA toxicity: bicarbonate reverses cardiac sodium channel blockade by raising serum pH and providing a sodium load. Australian thresholds for bicarbonate (eTG Toxicology, NSW Poisons Information Centre): QRS >100-120 ms, terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm, hypotension, broad-complex arrhythmia, or seizure. She meets multiple. Target QRS <120 ms, pH 7.50-7.55.
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed/unknown overdose (precipitates refractory seizures, especially in TCA where seizures already likely). (Source: NSW PIC).
Class III antiarrhythmics including amiodarone are contraindicated in TCA-induced wide-complex rhythms (further prolong QT, precipitate torsades). (Source: NSW PIC).
Gastric lavage is no longer recommended; charcoal at 90 min has limited benefit and unprotected airway in GCS 12 raises aspiration risk. (Source: NSW PIC).
Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose (associated with asystole and seizures); anticholinergic features are manifestation of broader toxicity. (Source: NSW PIC).

explanation.summary: Discontinuation syndrome (FINISH) develops within days of antidepressant dose reduction, is short-half-life-drug-prone (paroxetine, venlafaxine, duloxetine), lasts 1-2 weeks, and resolves on dose restoration. Relapse develops gradually over weeks with anhedonia and progressive functional decline (AMH; RANZCP).
key_points: FINISH: Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance (brain zaps), Hyperarousal
Onset within days, resolves within 1-2 weeks or immediately on dose restoration
Highest-risk agents: venlafaxine, paroxetine, duloxetine (short half-life)
Lowest-risk: fluoxetine (long half-life serves as self-taper)
Distinguish from relapse: rapid onset, sensory features, retained reactivity
explanation.pearls: Resolution within 24-48 hours of dose restoration confirms discontinuation rather than relapse (RANZCP).

options.rationale: Relapse of MDD typically develops over weeks not 48 h; includes core symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, neurovegetative) absent here. Would be correct with classic depressive features (Source: RANZCP).

Discontinuation syndrome: onset within days (typically 2-5 days) of dose reduction or cessation, FINISH mnemonic (Flu-like, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbance including brain zaps, Hyperarousal). Venlafaxine is among the highest-risk antidepressants due to short half-life (~5 hours parent, ~11 hours active metabolite). Management: reinstate previous dose, then taper more slowly. This is the AU-cutoff: venlafaxine taper steps should be smaller (37.5 mg) and more spaced than SSRIs.

Serotonin syndrome features hyperreflexia, clonus, hyperthermia and follows ADDITION of serotonergic agent, not dose REDUCTION. Would be correct with serotonergic addition (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines).
SNRIs do not cause hypothyroidism; no thyroid symptoms and no temporal link with dose change. (Source: AMH).
GAD requires 6+ months of pervasive worry with characteristic features; syndrome here is acute, sensorimotor and time-locked to dose reduction. (Source: DSM-5).

explanation.summary: Suicide risk is structured into static (chronic, non-modifiable: previous attempt, family history, male sex, mental illness) and dynamic (acute, modifiable: hopelessness, recent stressors, intoxication, means access, lack of social connection). Means restriction is the single most evidence-based modifiable acute factor in Australian and international guidelines (RANZCP; LIFE Framework).
key_points: Chronic non-modifiable: prior attempt, family history of suicide, male sex, chronic illness, prior trauma
Acute modifiable: means access, intoxication, recent stressors, hopelessness, lack of supports
Means restriction = highest-impact acute modifiable intervention
Safety plan: warning signs, internal coping, social distractors, supports, professional help, means restriction
Aboriginal mental health care: link with ACCHS for culturally safe follow-up
explanation.pearls: If a question lists access to a firearm or large medication stockpile, that is the modifiable factor to prioritise (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk
Australian Government LIFE: Living Is For Everyone Framework

options.rationale: Family history is non-modifiable distal risk factor; cannot be acted on to reduce acute risk. Would never be the modifiable answer (Source: RANZCP).
Identity is not a risk factor to be 'modified'; culturally-safe care and ACCHS linkage are the appropriate response, not pathologising identity. (Source: NACCHO).
source_refs: National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Suicide Prevention Strategy
RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Past self-harm is strong non-modifiable historical risk factor; cannot be addressed acutely to change risk. Would never be the modifiable answer (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Hopelessness is strongest psychological correlate of suicide and modifiable through therapy and treating mood disorder but in the discharge-window timeframe it cannot be eliminated; means restriction is the immediately modifiable factor (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Means restriction is the highest-evidence acute modifiable intervention in suicide prevention: removing or securing the firearm tonight (e.g. via partner-removal, police safe-storage, or temporary surrender) reduces lethality even if other risk factors persist. The acute window after presentation is when access to lethal means most strongly predicts completed suicide. RANZCP, Black Dog Institute and the National Suicide Prevention Strategy all rank means restriction as the most actionable acute step. (Resuming SSRI access and ACCHS linkage are also critical, but means restriction is rate-limiting.)

explanation.summary: After a self-harm presentation, collaborative safety planning (Stanley-Brown) combined with continuity of psychological care is evidence-based and reduces repeat suicidal behaviour. DBT chain analysis at the next session unpacks the precipitating chain. Involuntary admission, no-suicide contracts, and ED-initiated pharmacotherapy are not first-line (RANZCP; LIFE Framework).
key_points: Stanley-Brown Safety Plan: 6 components, collaboratively developed, written copy with patient
Continuity > containment: handover to established team is critical
No-suicide contracts have no evidence and may be harmful
BPD first-line treatment is structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, schema)
Chain analysis identifies vulnerabilities, precipitants, behaviour, consequences for skills practice
explanation.pearls: If a question describes superficial self-harm in a person with BPD and intact supports, safety plan + community handover beats admission (RANZCP).

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk
Australian Government LIFE: Living Is For Everyone Framework

options.rationale: Routine admission of BPD self-harm without acute suicide intent or psychosis worsens long-term outcomes (regression, role-reinforcement, iatrogenic harm). Would be correct only with acute suicide intent or psychosis (Source: NHMRC BPD).
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder 2013

options.rationale: 'No-suicide contracts' have NO evidence for reducing suicide risk and may worsen outcomes by substituting paper artefact for genuine engagement. (Source: NHMRC).

NHMRC BPD Guideline and the National Suicide Prevention Strategy endorse Stanley-Brown safety planning as the evidence-based ED discharge tool. The six steps include explicit means restriction and graded coping/social/professional escalation. Sharing the plan with her established DBT team preserves continuity of care, which is the active ingredient in BPD outcomes.
Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for BPD; medications target specific comorbidities not the disorder itself. Would be correct only for documented comorbid depression/psychosis (Source: NHMRC).

No alcohol or substances on board tonight and no documented substance-use comorbidity; mis-referral pathologises non-existent problem. Would be correct only with documented substance comorbidity (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Post-stroke depression affects ~30% of stroke survivors, peaks at 3-6 months, and worsens rehabilitation outcomes. Stroke Foundation Australia endorses SSRI plus active rehabilitation engagement as first-line. Sertraline or citalopram are preferred due to cardiovascular safety profile (Stroke Foundation; RANZCP).
key_points: PSD prevalence ~30%, peak 3-6 months
Australian first-line SSRI: sertraline or citalopram
Avoid TCAs in older post-stroke patients
Combine pharmacotherapy with active rehabilitation engagement
PHQ-9 may overestimate due to overlap with stroke-related items - interpret carefully
explanation.pearls: Untreated PSD worsens not just mood but motor and cognitive recovery (Stroke Foundation Australia).

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Post-stroke depression affects approximately 1 in 3 stroke survivors, peaks at 3-6 months, and meaningfully impairs rehabilitation outcomes. SSRI treatment (sertraline or citalopram are the preferred Australian first-line options for cardiovascular comorbidity) plus active rehabilitation engagement improves both mood and functional outcome. Combination beats either modality alone (Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines; RANZCP).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: PHQ-9 17 reflects moderate-to-severe depression with functional impact (refusing rehab, passive death thoughts); delaying treatment 3 months risks worse outcomes. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: Amitriptyline (TCA) has significant anticholinergic, orthostatic, cardiac risks in older post-stroke patients; sertraline or citalopram preferred. (Source: AMH).

ECT is for severe depression with catatonia, food/fluid refusal, high suicide risk, or treatment resistance; not first-line in moderate post-stroke depression. Would be correct in severe/treatment-resistant (Source: RANZCP).
Benzodiazepines in older adults increase falls, cognitive impairment and second stroke risk; not appropriate. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Perinatal mental health screening (EPDS, score >=13 prompts assessment) after pregnancy loss identifies treatable depression that should not be dismissed as 'normal grief'. COPE 2023 endorses combined SSRI plus structured psychotherapy with grief-informed peer support. Sertraline is the preferred Australian SSRI in perinatal contexts (COPE; RANZCP).
key_points: EPDS >=13 = positive screen; item 10 always reviewed for self-harm
Grief vs depression: grief is undulating; depression is pervasive with worthlessness and neurovegetative features
Sertraline is first-line Australian perinatal SSRI
SANDS and Red Nose are Australian bereavement supports
Prolonged grief disorder requires >=12 months in adults
explanation.pearls: After stillbirth, ask about EVERY pregnancy loss in subsequent years - anniversary reactions are common (COPE).

sources.label: COPE: Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period - Australian Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Her presentation goes beyond uncomplicated grief: EPDS 18 with item 10 positive, neurovegetative features, anhedonia, worthlessness, 6 weeks of impairment. Would be correct in uncomplicated grief (Source: COPE).
Prolonged grief disorder requires symptoms at least 12 months after loss in adults; she is at 6 weeks. Would be correct at 12+ months (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Benzodiazepines are not disease-modifying in MDD or grief, risk dependence, and may impair cognitive grief processing. (Source: COPE).

Combined antidepressant plus psychotherapy is recommended for moderate-to-severe perinatal MDD with item 10 positive on EPDS. Sertraline is first-line SSRI per COPE (her potential to breastfeed in future pregnancies makes sertraline a sensible default choice). Perinatal-experienced psychological therapy plus grief-informed peer support (SANDS Australia specifically supports stillbirth/neonatal loss) addresses both the MDE and the grief processes. Frequent GP review covers safety.
source_refs: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline 2023

options.rationale: Replacement child framing is contrary to perinatal bereavement guidance and risks complicated grief and PTSD in subsequent pregnancy. (Source: COPE).

explanation.summary: Adolescent-specific suicide risk factors include peer suicide bereavement (contagion), bullying (especially cyberbullying), gender and sexuality minority stress, family rejection, substance use, and impulsivity. The Australian Trans Pathways study documented dramatically elevated self-harm in transgender youth, largely modifiable by family acceptance, peer connectedness, and access to gender-affirming care. Multiple acute features mandate inpatient safety in this presentation (headspace; RANZCP; Trans Pathways).
key_points: HEEADSSS structures adolescent psychosocial screening
Adolescent-specific risks: peer suicide, bullying, identity-related stress, family rejection
LGBTQAI+ supports: QLife (1800 184 527), Twenty10, Minus18, headspace
Family acceptance is a strong protective factor for transgender youth
Mental Health Acts permit involuntary admission of minors when criteria met
explanation.pearls: Means restriction at home + LGBTQAI+ affirming care are two of the highest-yield modifiable interventions in transgender youth suicide prevention (Trans Pathways).

sources.label: headspace: youth mental health clinical guidance
RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Specific plan, available means at home, intended timing within 48 h with unsupervised window, recent bereavement by suicide, escalating bullying - discharge unsafe. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: headspace: youth mental health clinical guidance
RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Multiple acute high-risk features (specific plan + means + timing + recent peer suicide + active bullying + alienation from one parent + substance use + lack of professional supports) require an inpatient level of safety while initial assessment, family work, and treatment are established. Australian Mental Health Acts permit involuntary admission of minors when criteria are met. Affirming the young person's identity and connecting with LGBTQAI+ youth services (QLife, Twenty10, Minus18) is integral to care - gender minority youth suicide risk is elevated by family rejection and reduced by family acceptance, school connectedness, and culturally safe care (headspace; RANZCP; Trans Pathways).
source_refs: headspace: youth mental health clinical guidance
RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk

options.rationale: Fluoxetine is first-line for adolescent MDD but starting in ED with discharge into high acute-risk environment does not address immediate risk. Would be correct as part of inpatient plan (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).
Mandatory reporting applies where significant harm risk from a parent; mother is supportive and immediate risk is to self, not parental. (Source: NSW MRG).
source_refs: headspace: youth mental health clinical guidance

options.rationale: Specific plan, means, timing, recent peer suicide, active bullying are one of the highest-acuity adolescent presentations; minimising is dangerous. (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of suicide risk
headspace: youth mental health clinical guidance

explanation.summary: B12 deficiency is a high-yield psychiatric mimic in older adults, vegans, and those on chronic acid suppression. The diagnostic fingerprint integrates macrocytic anaemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + glossitis + selective dorsal column signs (subacute combined degeneration) + cognitive and mood symptoms. Australian workup pairs B12 with folate, ferritin, and confirmatory MMA/homocysteine; intrinsic factor antibodies define pernicious anaemia (Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; AMH).
key_points: High-risk groups: older adults, vegans, chronic PPI/H2RA, metformin, post-gastrectomy/bariatric, ileal disease
Subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception) + corticospinal tracts (brisk knee, absent ankle reflexes, Babinski)
Workup: B12, folate, ferritin; MMA and homocysteine if borderline; intrinsic factor antibodies for PA
Replacement: IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg alternate days for 2 weeks then 3-monthly (PA) or as required
Mood, psychosis, and cognitive symptoms can be the presenting feature - check B12 in any new geriatric mood or cognitive presentation
explanation.pearls: Brisk knee reflex WITH absent ankle reflex is the classic mixed-tract sign of subacute combined degeneration (Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Macrocytic anaemia (MCV 112) with hypersegmented neutrophils, glossitis, dorsal column signs (vibration/proprioception loss, Romberg positive), brisk knee + absent ankle reflexes (subacute combined degeneration pattern), cognitive impairment, mood and paranoid features in a long-term vegan ALSO on chronic PPI therapy is a textbook B12 deficiency. Australian first-line workup is serum B12 + folate; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine confirm intracellular deficiency when B12 is borderline. Intrinsic factor antibodies identify pernicious anaemia. Hypothyroidism is already excluded by current TSH (Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; AMH).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders overview

options.rationale: Vascular dementia can cause cognitive/mood symptoms but does NOT cause macrocytic anaemia, glossitis, hypersegmented neutrophils, or selective dorsal column signs. Would be correct in pure vascular cognitive impairment (Source: RANZCR).

Autoimmune encephalitis presents sub-acutely with psychiatric symptoms plus seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability; macrocytic anaemia and dorsal column signs do not fit. Would be correct with autoimmune encephalitis features (Source: Titulaer 2013).

TSH 1.8 within reference; hypothyroidism does not produce macrocytosis of this degree, hypersegmented neutrophils, glossitis, or dorsal column signs. Would be correct with biochemically active hypothyroidism (Source: APEG).

Weight loss has plausible nutritional explanation (long-term veganism, B12 deficiency, glossitis impairing eating); occult malignancy workup is reasonable later if B12 replacement does not resolve. Would be correct after B12 trial without response (Source: RACGP).

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal management in patients with normal hepatic function uses CIWA-Ar-guided diazepam loading (or scheduled diazepam in the severe-history group). The long half-life of diazepam provides a self-tapering effect, reducing both rebound and seizure risk. Severe hepatic dysfunction shifts choice to lorazepam (no active metabolite, glucuronidation rather than CYP). Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3 days precedes any carbohydrate load to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. CIWA-Ar score >=15 is severe and warrants more intensive management.
key_points: Diazepam-loading via CIWA-Ar in preserved hepatic function
Lorazepam in severe hepatic dysfunction (glucuronidation)
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV daily x 3 days before glucose
Long-acting benzodiazepines reduce seizure risk in withdrawal
Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold - avoid as primary agent
explanation.pearls: The classical revised CIWA-Ar covers 10 items including tremor, agitation, anxiety, sweats, nausea, headache, tactile/auditory/visual disturbances, and orientation; scoring guides individualised benzodiazepine dosing.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines 2008
NHMRC Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems 2021

options.rationale: Australian guidance (NSW Health, eTG Addiction Medicine) supports diazepam-loading guided by the revised Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) in patients with preserved hepatic function and a history of severe withdrawal or seizures. Diazepam's long half-life provides a 'self-tapering' profile and reduces seizure risk. Parenteral thiamine (300 mg IV daily for 3 days) precedes glucose administration to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy precipitated by carbohydrate-driven thiamine consumption.
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines 2008
NHMRC Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems 2021

options.rationale: Lorazepam (short-acting, no active metabolite) is preferred in significant hepatic dysfunction; this patient has normal LFTs and diazepam-loading is preferred for previous seizure history. Would be correct in severe liver disease (Source: eTG).
Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and do not address the GABAergic deficit driving withdrawal. Would be wrong as primary agent (Source: eTG).
Naltrexone is for relapse prevention once withdrawal is complete and the patient is abstinent; it does not treat acute withdrawal. Would be wrong timing (Source: AMH).
Glucose before thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede glucose. (Source: NSW Health).

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine choice in alcohol withdrawal is shaped by hepatic function. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide undergo phase I oxidative metabolism (CYP) and have active long-acting metabolites that accumulate in liver dysfunction. Lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam undergo only conjugation (glucuronidation), which is largely preserved in cirrhosis - hence the LOT mnemonic. Symptom-triggered dosing (CIWA-Ar) reduces total exposure compared with fixed-schedule dosing. Encephalopathy monitoring is critical to detect over-sedation.
key_points: Significant liver dysfunction: lorazepam preferred (glucuronidation only)
LOT mnemonic = Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam - safe in liver disease
Symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar dosing reduces total exposure
Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide accumulate in hepatic dysfunction
Encephalopathy monitoring critical for over-sedation detection
explanation.pearls: Hepatic encephalopathy and benzodiazepine over-sedation can look identical; structured monitoring (CIWA-Ar plus separate encephalopathy assessment) is essential.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines 2008

options.rationale: In significant hepatic dysfunction (cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B/C, elevated INR, encephalopathy), lorazepam is preferred because it is metabolised by conjugation (glucuronidation) rather than CYP-mediated oxidative phase I metabolism. This avoids the prolonged sedation and active-metabolite accumulation seen with diazepam (its active metabolites - desmethyldiazepam, oxazepam, temazepam - accumulate and prolong sedation, worsening encephalopathy assessment). Symptom-triggered dosing reduces total exposure.
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Guidelines 2008

options.rationale: Diazepam and its active metabolites accumulate in hepatic dysfunction, prolonging sedation and confounding encephalopathy assessment. Would be wrong in this hepatic context (Source: eTG).
Chlordiazepoxide has the same long-acting accumulation issue in liver disease as diazepam. (Source: AMH).
Midazolam IV infusion is for ICU-level sedation, not first-line ward withdrawal management; risks respiratory depression. (Source: AMH).
Clonidine treats autonomic symptoms but does not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines remain the GABAergic substitute. (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute thiamine-deficiency syndrome (classic triad: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion - though all three present in only ~10%), at risk of permanent Korsakoff syndrome if untreated. Prophylaxis in high-risk patients (alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery) is parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3 days, then oral 100 mg daily for 3-6 months. Thiamine MUST precede any glucose load. Anaphylaxis to IV thiamine is rare; oral B-complex is insufficient in alcohol-induced malabsorption.
key_points: 300 mg IV daily x 3 days prophylactic in high-risk
Thiamine BEFORE glucose, always
Classic triad in ~10% only - low threshold for treatment
Korsakoff is the irreversible end-state
Oral 100 mg daily for 3-6 months after parenteral phase
explanation.pearls: Therapeutic doses for established Wernicke encephalopathy are higher: 500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days, then taper - much higher than prophylactic doses.

sources.label: Royal College of Physicians Wernicke guideline

options.rationale: Australian guidance (eTG, NSW Health) and the Royal College of Physicians prophylactic protocol specify parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3 days for patients at high risk of Wernicke (alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hyperemesis, post-bariatric surgery) before any carbohydrate load. Glucose given to a thiamine-deficient brain consumes residual thiamine in pyruvate decarboxylation and transketolase reactions, precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Oral thiamine 100 mg daily continues for at least 3-6 months after the parenteral phase.
source_refs: Royal College of Physicians Wernicke guideline

options.rationale: Oral thiamine has poor bioavailability in chronic alcohol use due to gut malabsorption; parenteral loading is required for high-risk patients. (Source: eTG).
100 mg single dose is below the prophylactic threshold for at-risk patients; 300 mg IV daily for 3 days is the standard Australian regimen. Would be inadequate (Source: NSW Health).
Glucose given before thiamine in a deficient brain precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy by accelerating thiamine consumption. Would be unsafe (Source: eTG).

The classic triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion) is present in only ~10% of cases; prophylaxis is required in high-risk patients to prevent irreversible Korsakoff syndrome. Would be unsafe (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: Three pharmacotherapies are PBS-listed in Australia for AUD relapse prevention: naltrexone, acamprosate, and disulfiram. Naltrexone (mu-opioid antagonist) reduces heavy drinking; acamprosate (NMDA modulator/GABAergic) supports abstinence maintenance; disulfiram (aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor) creates aversive reaction with alcohol. Naltrexone and acamprosate are evidence-first-line; disulfiram is supervised-adherence-dependent. Combined psychosocial therapy improves outcomes for all three. Second-line: topiramate, gabapentin, baclofen (off-label in Australia).
key_points: First-line: naltrexone (heavy drinking reduction) or acamprosate (abstinence maintenance)
Disulfiram: aversive, requires supervised adherence
All three PBS-listed for AUD in Australia
Naltrexone contraindicated in concurrent opioid use
Combined with psychosocial therapy for best outcomes
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone before drinking ('targeted dosing' on heavy-drinking days) is evidence-supported for harm reduction rather than abstinence; this option fits patients not committed to total abstinence.

sources.label: NHMRC Australian guidelines for alcohol problems 2021

options.rationale: Oral naltrexone (a mu-opioid receptor antagonist) reduces heavy drinking days and risk of relapse to heavy drinking in alcohol use disorder, with Number Needed to Treat ~12 for return-to-any-drinking and ~20 for return-to-heavy-drinking (Jonas et al 2014 JAMA meta-analysis). Mechanism: blocking endogenous opioid reward from alcohol consumption. Contraindicated in concurrent opioid use (precipitated withdrawal) and severe hepatic dysfunction. PBS-listed for AUD in Australia.
source_refs: NHMRC Australian guidelines for alcohol problems 2021
Jonas DE et al. Pharmacotherapy for AUD. JAMA 2014

options.rationale: Acamprosate also has efficacy (NNT ~12 for abstinence maintenance) and is reasonable; naltrexone has slightly broader evidence for reducing heavy drinking. Acamprosate is preferred if abstinence-not-reduction is the goal and renal function is good. Would be wrong as 'most consistently demonstrated' but a reasonable alternative (Source: Jonas 2014).

Disulfiram works via aversive disulfiram-ethanol reaction (acetaldehyde accumulation) - evidence is mixed and depends on supervised adherence; effective in supervised settings but less robust overall. Would be wrong as 'most consistently demonstrated' (Source: NHMRC 2021).
SSRIs do not have demonstrated efficacy for AUD relapse prevention in the absence of comorbid depression. (Source: NHMRC).
Topiramate has growing evidence but is off-label in Australia for AUD and has cognitive and renal-stone tolerability issues; positioned second-line. Would be wrong as first-line (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Acamprosate is renally excreted unchanged; contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min, dose-reduced or avoided in mild-moderate impairment. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised; contraindicated in severe hepatic dysfunction or current opioid use. Choice of relapse-prevention pharmacotherapy is shaped by these comorbidities: liver disease without opioids favours acamprosate; renal disease without opioids favours naltrexone.
key_points: Acamprosate renally excreted; CrCl <30 contraindicated
Naltrexone hepatically metabolised; severe liver disease contraindicated
Current opioid use contraindicates naltrexone (precipitated withdrawal)
Comorbidity shapes choice, not blanket contraindication
Disulfiram requires supervision and motivation
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate has the unusual property of being almost completely unmetabolised - it is excreted unchanged in urine; this makes drug-drug interactions minimal but renal function critical.

options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally excreted unchanged; it is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min and cautioned in mild-moderate impairment with dose reduction or avoidance. eGFR 38 is borderline and most prescribers would prefer naltrexone (hepatic metabolism, normal LFTs here) given the renal context. Naltrexone is contraindicated in current opioid use (precipitated withdrawal) and severe hepatic dysfunction, neither of which applies.
Acamprosate is renally cleared and dose-relevant in renal impairment. (Source: AMH).
Routine combination is not standard; choose a single agent based on patient profile. (Source: NHMRC).
Naltrexone is metabolised hepatically; renal impairment does not contraindicate it. (Source: AMH).
Comorbidity informs choice but does not contraindicate all pharmacotherapy. (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Australian Opioid Treatment Program offers methadone (full mu-agonist), buprenorphine or buprenorphine-naloxone (partial mu-agonist), and depot buprenorphine (Sublocade, Buvidal). Methadone causes more sedation and QT prolongation; buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression (safer in overdose), less QT, lower sedation. Buprenorphine-naloxone reduces diversion via injection (naloxone precipitates withdrawal if injected). Induction requires sufficient opioid abstinence (~12-24 h since last short-acting opioid) to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
key_points: Methadone: full agonist, no ceiling on respiratory depression, QT risk
Buprenorphine: partial agonist, ceiling effect on respiratory depression
Buprenorphine-naloxone reduces diversion via injection
Induction needs opioid abstinence (12-24h short-acting, longer for methadone)
Depot buprenorphine (weekly/monthly) improves adherence
explanation.pearls: Buprenorphine's ceiling effect on respiratory depression is the main safety advantage over methadone - it explains the divergence of overdose mortality between the two when comparing OTP cohorts.

options.rationale: Buprenorphine (partial mu-opioid agonist) has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression making it safer in overdose, less QT impact than methadone, lower sedation, and the combined buprenorphine-naloxone product (Suboxone) discourages diversion via injection (naloxone has poor sublingual bioavailability but precipitates withdrawal if injected). His previous methadone sedation and QT prolongation favour switching. NSW OST clinics can supervise induction.
source_refs: NSW Health Opioid Treatment Program clinical guidelines

options.rationale: Methadone has caused QT prolongation and sedation in this patient; baseline QTc 470 ms is borderline and another methadone trial risks torsades. (Source: AMH).
Naltrexone requires complete opioid abstinence before initiation (would precipitate withdrawal); not appropriate as immediate OST. Would be wrong timing (Source: AMH).
Slow-release morphine is a niche third-line OST option in Australia, used when methadone and buprenorphine have failed; not first switch. (Source: eTG).
Codeine is not an evidence-based OST; not part of the Australian OTP. (Source: NSW Health).

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine induction timing prevents precipitated withdrawal. Buprenorphine's high mu-receptor affinity but partial agonism means it can displace a full agonist (heroin, methadone) and reduce net opioid activity, abruptly precipitating withdrawal. Protocol: wait until COWS >=12 (~12-24 h after short-acting opioid, 36-72+ h after methadone), then induce with small initial doses (e.g. 2-4 mg) titrated upward. Micro-dosing protocols (Bernese method) are specialist-led alternatives for patients who cannot tolerate withdrawal before induction.
key_points: Buprenorphine partial agonist + high affinity = precipitated withdrawal risk
Wait for COWS >=12 before induction
12-24 h post short-acting opioid; 36-72+ h post methadone
Start 2-4 mg sublingual, titrate by symptoms
Micro-dosing (Bernese) is specialist option
explanation.pearls: Precipitated withdrawal is distressing and can prematurely end an induction attempt - patient engagement and trust are damaged; cautious timing is therapeutic alliance protection.

options.rationale: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial mu-agonist that displaces full agonists (heroin, methadone) from receptors. If administered while a full agonist still occupies receptors, the substitution reduces net opioid activity, precipitating withdrawal. Standard practice is to wait until objective withdrawal is present (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale - COWS - score >=12) before starting buprenorphine, typically 12-24 hours after last short-acting opioid and longer (36-72 hours or more) after methadone.
Administering before withdrawal is established risks precipitated withdrawal, with abrupt distressing symptoms. (Source: eTG).
Methadone induction also requires careful titration; switching the agent does not solve the timing issue and was not the agreed plan. (Source: NSW Health OTP).
Naloxone would precipitate immediate severe withdrawal and is not part of induction; nonsensical here. (Source: AMH).

Even small doses of buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal in a recently-dosed opioid user; the protocol is to wait, not to test with micro-dose in standard induction. Note: micro-dosing protocols exist but are specialist-led and not first-line for typical heroin users (Source: NSW Health OTP).

explanation.summary: Opioid overdose causes death by respiratory depression; naloxone (mu-opioid antagonist) is the targeted reversal. Titrate in small aliquots (0.1-0.4 mg IV) to restore adequate ventilation (RR >=12), not to full consciousness, to avoid precipitated withdrawal and patient self-discharge. Naloxone half-life (60-90 min) is shorter than most opioids (especially long-acting agents like methadone), so observation, repeat boluses, or infusion may be needed. Take-home naloxone (intranasal Nyxoid, Prenoxad IM) is a key harm reduction intervention.
key_points: Opioid toxidrome: pinpoint pupils + bradypnoea + reduced consciousness
Titrate naloxone 0.1-0.4 mg IV; goal is ventilation, not waking
Naloxone half-life shorter than most opioids - observation required
Methadone and long-acting opioids: prolonged monitoring
Take-home naloxone is high-yield harm reduction
explanation.pearls: Methadone overdose can re-sedate after initial naloxone wears off; ICU observation up to 24 hours may be required, sometimes with naloxone infusion.

options.rationale: Opioid overdose causes death by respiratory depression. Immediate priority is ventilation; naloxone (mu-opioid receptor antagonist) is titrated in small aliquots (0.1-0.4 mg IV) to restore adequate respiration (RR >=12, SpO2 acceptable), not to full consciousness. Full waking precipitates abrupt withdrawal, distress, and patient self-discharge before safe redosing as naloxone half-life (60-90 min) is shorter than most opioids. Repeat boluses or infusion may be needed.
Large bolus precipitates abrupt withdrawal, vomiting (aspiration), agitation, and patient self-discharge before redose. (Source: eTG).
Naloxone is the targeted reversal agent and avoids intubation when effective; ventilation is the bridge, not the destination. (Source: eTG).
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids; pinpoint pupils + bradypnoea = opioid toxidrome. (Source: AMH).
Activated charcoal is for recent oral overdose with intact airway; this is parenteral overdose with airway compromise. (Source: NSW PIC).

explanation.summary: Acute methamphetamine intoxication presents with sympathomimetic features (hyperthermia, hypertension, tachycardia, mydriasis, diaphoresis) plus psychomotor agitation and frequently psychosis. Management: ventilation/airway, active cooling, IV fluids, IV benzodiazepines titrated for the sympathetic drive and seizure prophylaxis, IM olanzapine for the psychotic/agitated component if IV access is unavailable. Do NOT combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour. Avoid beta-blocker monotherapy (unopposed alpha stimulation). Methamphetamine-induced psychosis often resolves over hours to days; persistent psychosis warrants psychiatric review.
key_points: Methamphetamine = sympathomimetic + psychomotor + psychosis
First-line: benzodiazepines IV titrated (when access available)
IM olanzapine for psychotic/agitated component without IV access
Do not combine IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour
Avoid beta-blocker monotherapy
explanation.pearls: HNE LHD has high rates of methamphetamine presentations; ED training pathways embed these specific drug-on-drug timing rules.

options.rationale: In methamphetamine-induced acute behavioural disturbance with combined psychosis and sympathomimetic features, NSW Health and HNE LHD pathways support either IM olanzapine (preferred in this scenario where psychotic features are prominent and IV access is not yet available) or IV benzodiazepine titration once access is in place. The two are not combined within 1 hour due to combined cardiorespiratory depression risk. The plan is to secure IV access in parallel and add titrated benzodiazepine after the olanzapine window if sympathomimetic features predominate.
source_refs: HNE LHD acute behavioural disturbance pathway

options.rationale: Combining IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine within 1 hour increases cardiorespiratory depression and is explicitly avoided in NSW guidance. (Source: NSW Health).
Haloperidol carries higher QT prolongation risk than olanzapine and methamphetamine itself can prolong QT; without ECG support, haloperidol is not preferred. (Source: AMH).
Active cooling is necessary alongside but does not address agitation, sympathetic drive or psychosis; required as adjunct, not alone. Would be incomplete (Source: NSW PIC).
Beta-blockade in unopposed alpha stimulation (methamphetamine) risks worsening hypertension; avoided. (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: Substance-induced psychotic disorder (DSM-5) resolves within 1 month of cessation; persistence beyond that, or features of primary psychosis (negative symptoms, prodrome, family history, prior episodes off substance), shift the diagnostic frame to primary psychotic disorder. Best practice is to treat acute symptoms, observe over the substance-withdrawal window, and reassess before committing to a primary diagnosis and long-term antipsychotic. Approximately 20-30% of patients with stimulant-induced psychosis develop a primary psychotic illness on longitudinal follow-up.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within 1 month of cessation
Persistence beyond 1 month -> primary diagnosis
20-30% of stimulant-induced psychosis develops primary illness
Acute antipsychotic for distressing symptoms is appropriate
Follow-up engagement essential
explanation.pearls: Cannabis-induced psychosis has a similar pattern but a higher conversion rate to primary psychosis (~40% in some cohorts), particularly in youth onset and high-potency use.

sources.label: Bramness JG et al. Amphetamine-induced psychosis. BMC Psychiatry 2012

options.rationale: Methamphetamine-induced psychosis typically resolves within days to a few weeks of abstinence, with the majority resolving in under a month. DSM-5 distinguishes substance-induced psychotic disorder (resolves within a month of withdrawal) from primary psychotic disorder. Premature commitment to a primary psychosis diagnosis and indefinite antipsychotic may pathologise a self-limiting drug effect; persistence beyond 4 weeks of abstinence (or earlier in the presence of strong primary-illness features) warrants formal primary diagnosis.
source_refs: Bramness JG et al. Amphetamine-induced psychosis. BMC Psychiatry 2012

options.rationale: Substance-induced psychosis often resolves; premature diagnosis pathologises self-limiting features. (Source: DSM-5-TR).
Follow-up is essential to distinguish substance-induced from primary illness and to engage with substance treatment. (Source: RANZCP).
Acute antipsychotic for distressing psychotic symptoms during the acute phase is appropriate; the question is about long-term diagnosis and treatment, not acute refusal. (Source: RANZCP).
Strong positive urine drug screen + temporal relationship is supportive of substance-induced; default-to-primary inverts the diagnostic logic. (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: AUDIT-C is a 3-item brief screen for hazardous alcohol use, derived from the full 10-item AUDIT. Cut-offs: >=4 for men and >=3 for women for hazardous use; positive screen prompts full AUDIT and brief intervention. RACGP and NHMRC support its use in opportunistic primary care screening. CAGE was an earlier tool focused on dependence rather than hazardous use, with reduced sensitivity in women and young people.
key_points: AUDIT-C: 3 items, brief screen for hazardous use
Cut-off: >=4 men, >=3 women
Positive screen prompts full AUDIT + brief intervention
CAGE outdated; less sensitive in women and youth
Australian standard drink = 10g pure alcohol
explanation.pearls: NHMRC 2021 alcohol guidelines: no more than 10 standard drinks per week and no more than 4 in any single day, for both men and women; this is a shift from the previous sex-differentiated 2009 thresholds.

options.rationale: AUDIT-C is the 3-item brief alcohol screen derived from the full 10-item AUDIT, validated in primary care for hazardous drinking detection. Cut-offs for hazardous use are >=4 for men and >=3 for women in most validation studies; higher cut-offs (>=5/>=4) increase specificity for AUD. RACGP and NHMRC guidance support AUDIT-C as a brief opportunistic primary care screen.
source_refs: NHMRC Australian guidelines for alcohol problems 2021
Bush K et al. AUDIT-C validation Arch Intern Med 1998

options.rationale: CAGE detects established alcohol dependence rather than hazardous drinking and is less sensitive in women and young people; AUDIT-C is preferred for opportunistic primary care screening (Source: RACGP).
The full AUDIT is longer than needed for an opportunistic brief screen; AUDIT-C is the validated brief 3-item version specifically designed for primary care (Source: NHMRC).
GAD-7 is a validated screen for generalised anxiety disorder and does not assess alcohol consumption; an inappropriate tool for hazardous drinking detection (Source: Spitzer 2006).
PHQ-9 is a validated screen for depression and does not assess alcohol consumption; an inappropriate tool for hazardous drinking detection (Source: Kroenke 2001).

explanation.summary: OST in pregnancy is recommended over no OST in opioid-dependent women; abrupt unsupervised withdrawal risks fetal stress and miscarriage. Both methadone and buprenorphine are acceptable under specialist supervision. The MOTHER trial (Jones HE et al NEJM 2010) showed buprenorphine associated with shorter neonatal abstinence syndrome treatment duration and length of stay compared with methadone, though similar overall obstetric outcomes. Neonatal team awareness for NAS is essential; breastfeeding is generally encouraged while on either agent.
key_points: OST recommended over no OST in opioid-dependent pregnant women
Both methadone and buprenorphine acceptable
Buprenorphine: shorter NAS treatment duration (MOTHER trial)
Avoid rapid detoxification (fetal stress)
Breastfeeding generally encouraged on OST
explanation.pearls: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS) is more about postnatal management (Finnegan scoring, morphine or methadone taper) than antenatal choice; both agents allow successful neonatal weaning.

sources.label: Jones HE et al. MOTHER trial NEJM 2010

options.rationale: Both methadone and buprenorphine are recommended in pregnancy under specialist supervision; opioid substitution therapy reduces obstetric and neonatal complications compared with continued unstructured use or unsupervised withdrawal. Buprenorphine is associated with somewhat less severe neonatal abstinence syndrome (MOTHER trial 2010, Jones et al NEJM), but methadone has the longer historical evidence base. Choice depends on prior experience, retention, and clinical context. Avoid abrupt unsupervised withdrawal (risk of fetal stress and miscarriage).
source_refs: Jones HE et al. MOTHER trial NEJM 2010

options.rationale: OST is recommended in pregnancy; unsupervised withdrawal carries fetal stress and miscarriage risk and ongoing unstructured use carries higher fetal harm. (Source: RANZCOG).
Naltrexone is not recommended in pregnancy; lacks safety evidence and risks precipitated withdrawal. (Source: AMH).
Rapid detoxification is not recommended in pregnancy; risk of fetal stress and miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG).
Deferring leaves the mother and fetus exposed to unstructured use; antenatal OST initiation is recommended. (Source: NSW Health OTP).

explanation.summary: GHB (gamma-hydroxybutyrate) is a GABA-B (and weak GABA-A) agonist with a very short half-life; daily-frequent use builds rapid tolerance, and abrupt cessation produces a severe withdrawal syndrome (autonomic instability, agitation, delirium, sometimes psychosis or seizures) that can progress rapidly. Management is inpatient with high-dose benzodiazepine substitution titrated to symptoms; refractory cases may require barbiturate or propofol sedation under HDU/ICU care. The short half-life of GHB means symptoms can escalate within hours of cessation, unlike the longer alcohol withdrawal trajectory.
key_points: GHB has very short half-life - withdrawal escalates fast
Severe withdrawal can be delirium with autonomic storm
Management: inpatient + high-dose benzodiazepines + HDU/ICU monitoring
Refractory: phenobarbital or propofol
Outpatient withdrawal unsafe
explanation.pearls: GHB withdrawal is often under-recognised in EDs because the patient may not disclose use; clinicians should consider GHB withdrawal when a young patient presents with severe agitation/autonomic features and no obvious alcohol or stimulant history.

options.rationale: GHB has a short half-life (~30 min) and induces severe withdrawal that can progress rapidly to a delirium with autonomic instability, requiring HDU/ICU-level care. Management is high-dose benzodiazepines titrated to symptoms; benzodiazepine-refractory cases may need barbiturate (phenobarbital) or propofol sedation under intensive care. Mortality without aggressive management is non-trivial. Outpatient withdrawal is not appropriate.
Severe GHB withdrawal is not safely managed as outpatient; admission required. (Source: eTG).
Naltrexone is opioid-targeted, not relevant in GHB withdrawal; the priority is acute withdrawal management. (Source: AMH).
Beta-blocker addresses symptoms without treating underlying GABAergic deficit; benzodiazepines are the substrate substitution. Would be wrong as primary therapy (Source: eTG).
GHB has no medical prescribing role for substitution; substitution is via benzodiazepines (GABA-A activity overlap). (Source: eTG).

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine cessation requires gradual taper (~10% of current dose every 2-4 weeks, longer plateaus at lower doses, total 6-12+ months) to minimise seizure risk and rebound symptoms. Switching short-acting agents (alprazolam, lorazepam, oxazepam) to diazepam-equivalent first smooths the taper because of diazepam's long half-life. Psychological support reduces relapse. Patients often experience protracted withdrawal symptoms (mood, sleep, cognitive) for weeks to months beyond the taper.
key_points: ~10% reduction of current dose every 2-4 weeks
Longer plateaus at lower doses (proportional reductions get larger)
Total taper 6-12+ months for long-term users
Switch short-acting to diazepam first if needed
Psychological support reduces relapse
explanation.pearls: The Ashton manual is the most widely referenced patient-facing tapering resource; many GPs share it with patients during deprescribing.

options.rationale: Long-term benzodiazepine withdrawal requires very gradual tapering to minimise seizures, rebound anxiety/insomnia, and protracted withdrawal symptoms. Australian and Ashton-manual-based guidance suggests reducing by approximately 10% of the current dose every 2-4 weeks, with longer plateaus at lower doses (because each mg drop is a larger proportion). Total taper duration is typically 6-12+ months for long-term users. Switching to a long-acting equivalent (diazepam) before tapering is helpful for short-acting agents (lorazepam, oxazepam, alprazolam).
source_refs: Ashton C. Benzodiazepines: how they work and how to withdraw

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after 15 years risks seizures and severe rebound; gradual taper required. (Source: RACGP).
50% weekly reduction is too rapid for long-term users; symptoms and seizure risk are substantial. (Source: eTG).
Propranolol masks autonomic symptoms but does not prevent seizures; rapid cessation is still unsafe. (Source: AMH).
Alprazolam is short-acting and more difficult to taper; switching FROM diazepam TO alprazolam inverts the recommended approach. (Source: Ashton).

explanation.summary: Cannabis use disorder is treated first-line with psychological intervention (CBT, motivational enhancement, contingency management). Cannabis withdrawal (irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, appetite change, restlessness, craving) is recognised in DSM-5; peaks days 2-4, resolves 1-2 weeks. No pharmacotherapy is first-line in Australia; symptomatic support and engagement with psychological treatment are core. Acknowledgement that withdrawal is real and time-limited reduces relapse.
key_points: First-line: CBT, motivational enhancement, contingency management
Cannabis withdrawal is DSM-5 recognised - real, time-limited
Peaks days 2-4, resolves 1-2 weeks
No first-line pharmacotherapy in Australia
Validation of withdrawal symptoms reduces relapse
explanation.pearls: Vivid dreams in cannabis withdrawal reflect REM-rebound after chronic suppression of REM sleep; warning patients about this in advance frames the symptom as expected, not catastrophic.

options.rationale: Cannabis withdrawal (irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance with vivid dreams, appetite loss, restlessness) typically peaks at days 2-4 and resolves within 1-2 weeks; recognition prevents relapse. First-line management is psychological (CBT, motivational enhancement, contingency management) with symptomatic support; no pharmacotherapy is approved as first-line in Australia for cannabis use disorder. Nabiximols and other agents have been trialled but are not standard practice.
source_refs: Allsop DJ et al. Cannabis Withdrawal Scale

options.rationale: Naltrexone is for alcohol and opioid use disorders, not cannabis. (Source: AMH).
Medicinal cannabis as substitution therapy for cannabis use disorder is not standard practice and lacks evidence-based positioning. (Source: NHMRC).
Long-term benzodiazepines create dependence; not first-line for cannabis withdrawal. (Source: AMH).

Quetiapine off-label for sleep is not appropriate; brief sleep hygiene and short-term benzodiazepine alternative (e.g. mirtazapine if needed) are preferred. Would be wrong as first-line (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Best-practice AUD care for Aboriginal patients integrates evidence-based pharmacotherapy with culturally safe psychosocial care, ideally delivered through Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services (Aboriginal Medical Services). Community-based care, family involvement with consent, and recognition of intergenerational trauma improve engagement. Pharmacotherapy access should not be restricted by demographic. NHMRC and NACCHO guidance align on these principles.
key_points: Evidence-based pharmacotherapy + culturally safe psychosocial care
AMS settings improve engagement and retention
Family involvement with consent
Recognise intergenerational trauma
Avoid removal from community where possible
explanation.pearls: Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services have demonstrated better engagement and outcomes than mainstream services for many conditions; refer locally where available.

options.rationale: NHMRC 2021 alcohol guidelines and Aboriginal-specific resources support evidence-based pharmacotherapy (naltrexone or acamprosate) alongside culturally safe psychosocial care delivered through Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services where possible. Engagement of family with consent reinforces support networks central to Aboriginal cultural frameworks. AMS settings reduce barriers and improve retention.
source_refs: NHMRC Australian guidelines for alcohol problems 2021
RACGP National guide to a preventive health assessment for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is evidence-based for AUD and access should not be restricted by demographic. (Source: NHMRC).
Mandatory removal from community is not culturally safe; community-based care where possible improves engagement. (Source: NACCHO).
Disulfiram requires established abstinence before initiation and supervised adherence; not first-line as initial approach. (Source: AMH).
Brief intervention is appropriate for hazardous use but inadequate for established AUD with previous relapse; longitudinal pharmacological + psychosocial care is required. (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Disulfiram has multiple important interactions beyond the well-known disulfiram-ethanol reaction (acetaldehyde accumulation when alcohol is consumed). Metronidazole + disulfiram has been associated with acute confusional/psychotic states; the combination is to be avoided. Other relevant interactions include warfarin (increased INR), phenytoin (raised levels), and isoniazid (CNS toxicity). Disulfiram's effect persists up to 14 days after cessation due to irreversible aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition.
key_points: Disulfiram + metronidazole: confusional/psychotic state - avoid
Disulfiram effect persists up to 14 days after cessation
Other key interactions: warfarin, phenytoin, isoniazid
Disulfiram-ethanol reaction is the named one but not the only one
Choose alternative antibiotic; do not pause disulfiram briefly
explanation.pearls: Hidden alcohol in pharmaceuticals (some elixirs, mouthwashes, cough syrups) can precipitate disulfiram-ethanol reaction; patient education and pharmacy alert are part of care.

options.rationale: Metronidazole combined with disulfiram has been associated with acute confusion, psychosis and seizures (the mechanism is thought to involve compound dopamine-beta-hydroxylase inhibition leading to dopamine accumulation and noradrenaline depletion in the CNS). The combination is contraindicated in many references; alternative antimicrobials should be chosen. This is independent of the well-known disulfiram-ethanol reaction (acetaldehyde accumulation when alcohol is consumed on disulfiram).
Combination has caused confusional psychosis and is to be avoided; not safe. (Source: AMH).

Disulfiram has prolonged effect (up to 14 days post-cessation); brief pause does not eliminate interaction risk and disrupts AUD maintenance. Choosing an alternative antimicrobial is preferred. (Source: AMH).
Permanent cessation removes a maintenance therapy without need; switching the antibiotic is the simpler, safer change. (Source: AMH).
Benzodiazepine prophylaxis does not prevent the disulfiram-metronidazole CNS effect and adds its own risks. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Varenicline (alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic partial agonist) has the strongest single-pharmacotherapy evidence for smoking cessation (~3x quitting odds vs placebo). Combined NRT (patch + faster-onset form) approaches varenicline efficacy. Earlier neuropsychiatric safety concerns (which led to a US boxed warning) were not confirmed in the EAGLES trial (Anthenelli NEJM 2016) and the warning was removed. Australian RACGP guidelines now position varenicline and combined NRT as first-line.
key_points: Varenicline most effective single agent (~3x placebo)
Combined NRT (patch + faster-onset) close second
Bupropion alternative
EAGLES (2016) cleared neuropsychiatric concerns
Behavioural support adds to all pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Set the quit date for day 8-14 of varenicline therapy; patient smokes the first week to build receptor occupancy before quit day - this is the licensed protocol.

sources.label: Anthenelli RM et al. EAGLES. NEJM 2016

options.rationale: Varenicline (alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic partial agonist) is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation (~3x odds of quitting vs placebo), outperforming single-form NRT and bupropion in head-to-head Cochrane network meta-analyses (Cahill et al). Earlier safety signals for neuropsychiatric events were not confirmed in the EAGLES trial (Anthenelli et al NEJM 2016). Combined NRT (patch + faster-onset gum/lozenge) approaches varenicline efficacy and is the second choice.
source_refs: Cahill K et al. Cochrane network meta-analysis 2013
Anthenelli RM et al. EAGLES. NEJM 2016

options.rationale: Single-form NRT alone has been tried twice without success; escalation to combined NRT or varenicline is appropriate. (Source: RACGP).
Bupropion is effective but less so than varenicline or combined NRT; appropriate as alternative. Would be less optimal first choice (Source: Cahill 2013).
E-cigarettes are not first-line pharmacotherapy in Australia; varenicline and NRT are evidence-based first-line. (Source: RACGP).
Hypnosis lacks robust evidence as the primary modality; pharmacotherapy is recommended. (Source: Cochrane).

explanation.summary: Successful cessation of methadone maintenance requires very gradual taper (2-5 mg every 2-4 weeks, smaller decrements at lower doses) and continued psychosocial engagement. Relapse rates are high regardless of pace (60-80% in most cohorts) - patients should be counselled about this and offered re-engagement with OST without judgment if they relapse. Naltrexone post-cessation can reduce relapse but requires 7-10 days opioid-free first.
key_points: Very gradual taper: 2-5 mg every 2-4 weeks
Slower at lower doses; longer plateaus
Relapse high (60-80%) regardless of pace
Naltrexone option post-cessation (7-10 days opioid-free first)
Ultra-rapid detoxification under anaesthesia not recommended
explanation.pearls: Patient-driven taper with the ability to pause or reverse the decrement when struggling has the best retention; rigid externally-imposed tapers fail more often.

options.rationale: Successful opioid maintenance cessation requires very gradual tapering (typically 2-5 mg every 2-4 weeks, with longer plateaus and smaller reductions at lower doses) and continued psychosocial engagement. Relapse risk is high (>=60-80% in many cohorts) regardless of pace, but slower tapers and continued support reduce attrition. Naltrexone may be considered after complete cessation to reduce relapse, but requires 7-10 days opioid-free first to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
Rapid taper has high relapse rate; not recommended for long-term users. (Source: NSW OTP).

Switching to buprenorphine before cessation can be appropriate to ease taper but immediate cessation post-switch is not the recommended approach; gradual taper still needed. Would be wrong as plan (Source: eTG).
Ultra-rapid detoxification under anaesthesia is no longer recommended (high relapse, complications, deaths reported). (Source: NHMRC).
Naltrexone after cold turkey requires 7-10 opioid-free days; starting on top of methadone precipitates severe withdrawal. (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: An Australian standard drink contains 10 g of pure alcohol. To estimate the standard drinks in any beverage: volume (mL) x %ABV x 0.789 (ethanol density g/mL) divided by 10. For a 750 mL bottle at 13% ABV: 750 x 0.13 x 0.789 / 10 = 7.7 standard drinks (~8). NHMRC 2021 guidelines limit healthy adults to no more than 10 standard drinks per week and no more than 4 in any single day.
key_points: 1 standard drink Australia = 10 g pure alcohol
Calculation: mL x %ABV x 0.789 / 10
Wine 750 mL bottle at 13% ~ 8 standard drinks
NHMRC 2021: <=10/week, <=4/day for both sexes
Always include the calculation in alcohol counselling
explanation.pearls: Patients consistently underestimate their consumption when using 'glasses' as the unit - explicit calculation of standard drinks per typical pour reveals the actual intake.

options.rationale: An Australian standard drink contains 10 g of pure alcohol. Calculation: 750 mL x 0.13 x 0.789 g/mL (ethanol density) = approximately 77 g pure alcohol, which equates to approximately 7.7 standard drinks (rounded to 8). This is a foundational calculation for alcohol counselling, and underpins NHMRC 2021 guideline limits (<= 10 standard drinks/week and <= 4 on any single day for both men and women).
2 standard drinks would be ~20 g alcohol, which is far below the actual alcohol content of a 750 mL bottle at 13%. Would be wrong on arithmetic (Source: NHMRC).
Underestimate; 40 g alcohol corresponds to roughly half a bottle at 13%. (Source: NHMRC).
Overestimate; 12 standard drinks = 120 g alcohol, which is more than a 750 mL bottle at 13%. (Source: NHMRC).
Substantial overestimate; not plausible for 750 mL at 13%. (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Australian suicide-risk practice has moved from categorical low/medium/high stratification to structured assessment of ideation severity, intent, plan, behaviour, dynamic and static risk factors, and access to means, with safety planning tailored to modifiable drivers. The C-SSRS is the most widely used structured framework, with the Chronological Assessment of Suicide Events (CASE) approach as the complementary interview technique.
key_points: Categorical low/medium/high stratification is deprecated
C-SSRS separates ideation by intent and plan and counts behaviours
Static factors set baseline risk; dynamic factors are what intervention targets
Access to means (firearms, medications) must be addressed
Family history of suicide is a non-trivial static risk factor
explanation.pearls: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea; explicit, calm questioning increases disclosure.

sources.label: NSW Health Suicide Risk Assessment and Management Framework

options.rationale: The Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) is the structured framework most widely endorsed in Australian and international guidance: it separates passive ideation, active ideation without plan, ideation with method, ideation with intent, and ideation with plan-and-intent, then enumerates preparatory acts and interrupted, aborted and actual attempts. It captures both severity and behaviour rather than yielding a single risk score and is the basis for triage decisions across NSW Health mental health services.
source_refs: NSW Health Suicide Risk Assessment and Management Framework
